title: How to pass this in a weekend
lead:
You have not read this course and the exam is on Tuesday. That is fine.
This book is built for exactly that. It ignores everything the exam will not ask and
teaches you, from zero, the dozen skills that answer every question. Do what it says and
you will walk in ready.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: The one idea behind this book
blocks.html: Computer Architecture looks huge but the exam is small. It reuses about a dozen ideas, over and over, with the numbers changed. So this book does not try to cover the syllabus. It works backwards from the exam: it takes the real questions as the target, then teaches every skill you need to reach them, starting from nothing. Each skill is taught so you understand why it works, not just what to write, which is the only way to stay safe when the examiner changes the numbers on you.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: The habit that passes the exam
blocks.html:
Reading feels like studying and teaches you almost nothing. What puts a skill into your hands is doing it with the answer covered. So all through this book you will meet two things, and you must actually use them:

  • A Your turn box: a question with new numbers and the answer hidden under a dashed line. Cover it, work it on paper, then check. This is where the learning happens.
  • After a worked example, Now redo it: close the book and reproduce the whole solution on blank paper. If you can do that, you own the skill.

The rule: never move on from a skill until you can do its Your-turn box cold, from memory, with different numbers. That single habit is the difference between a pass and a blank page.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Two kinds of question, and this book prepares you for both:

  • Objective questions (MCQs). Multiple choice, one right answer out of four. The lecturer has said these are coming. They test definitions and quick judgement across the whole course. Every one from the practice tests is answered and explained in Part C.
  • The written paper. The classic shape is Question One, compulsory, 30 marks, then any two of the remaining questions at 20 marks each, for 70 marks in 2 hours. Question One is where the number-crunching lives, so master it and you have half the paper before you choose anything. The whole 2025/2026 paper is worked at the back as your final mock.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.html:
Three days, three sittings. Do the Your-turn boxes as you go, do not just read.

  • Saturday, Part A. The big picture, then all the number skills: number systems, signed numbers, floating point, and image sizing. These are pure marks and most of the numeric MCQs.
  • Sunday, Part B. The machine: instruction formats, addressing modes, CPU performance, pipelining, and memory and cache. This is the heart of Question One.
  • Monday, Part C. The last of the theory, then work the whole MCQ bank as a test, then sit the 2025/2026 paper under the clock. Spend the evening redoing anything you got wrong.

If you are short on time, the order is chosen so the earliest sections are the highest value. Never skip Part A: everything else stands on it.

title: The Big Picture
lead:
Before any sums, the shape of the whole thing. Half the objective questions
live right here: what a computer is made of, and the one distinction the examiner asks in a
dozen disguises, architecture versus organization.

blocks.label: What a computer is, and what this course asks of you
blocks.html:
Start with the machine in front of you. Whatever you are reading this on, it is doing one thing over and over: taking in data, working on it according to instructions it has stored, and giving something back.

The lecturer gives that idea three times, each a little sharper, and the exam quotes all three.

DefinitionThe word it adds
1A computer is a programmable device that stores, retrieves and processes dataProgrammable. Change the program, change the job
2A machine or device that performs processes, calculations and operations based on instructions provided by a software or hardware programInstructions. Somebody told it what to do
3A sophisticated electronic calculating machine that accepts data, processes it according to a list of internally stored instructions, and produces the resulting output informationInternally stored. The instructions live inside it
Read the three together and you have the whole course

Accept data. Store instructions. Process. Output.
That third definition is the stored-program idea you are about to meet by name, written out in plain English before anybody calls it Von Neumann.

The parts, and why one example covers them all. For the most part every personal computer is built from the same basic components:

  • the Central Processing Unit, the CPU
  • memory
  • the circuit board that carries everything
  • storage
  • input and output devices

Almost every digital device uses that same set, which is why examining one personal computer gives you insight into a phone, a router, a car engine controller and a cash machine alike. Think about a computer in terms of its basic components and the job each one does, and the primary functions of computers in general come out of it.

Why any of it matters. Computers have changed the way society operates, and the efficiency gained through automation and organisation only scratches the surface of what the technology has given us. It has moved far enough that a business NOT using computing technology is now at a disadvantage against one that does.

What this course covers, so you know what the paper can ask: the relationship between hardware and software, the organisation of the CPU, the memory hierarchy, input and output mechanisms, instruction execution, and performance measurement. By the end you should be able to say how computers are designed, how they execute programs, and how architectural choices affect performance.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A computer runs a program by repeating three steps forever: it fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it (works out what it means), then executes it, and loops back to do it all again. That never-ending loop is the fetch, decode, execute cycle.
frames.ask: Name the three steps, in order.

frames.teach: Where do those instructions live? In memory, written as plain binary numbers, sitting right beside the data they work on. This one idea, the program and the data together in the same memory, is the stored-program (or Von Neumann) concept.
frames.ask:
Are the program and the
data kept in the same memory, or in two separate ones?

frames.teach: That is exactly what makes a computer general: change the numbers in memory and the same machine does a different job. Now look inside the processor, the CPU. Its first working part is the control unit (CU), the conductor: it fetches each instruction and sends out the control signals that make everything act at the right moment.
frames.ask:
Does the CU itself do the adding and
subtracting, yes or no?

frames.teach: The adding, subtracting, AND, OR and comparing is the job of the second part, the arithmetic and logic unit (ALU). So keep the two apart: the CU directs, the ALU calculates.
frames.ask:
Which unit actually works
out 7 + 5?

frames.teach: The CPU also keeps a few tiny, very fast stores called registers, each holding something it needs right now. The first is the program counter (PC): it holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.
frames.ask: What does the PC hold?

frames.check: the address of the next instruction.
frames.teach: Once an instruction has been fetched, it is held in the instruction register (IR) while it is decoded and run.
frames.ask:
Which register holds the instruction currently being
executed?

frames.teach: Two more registers, both for talking to memory. The memory address register (MAR) holds the address the CPU is about to read from or write to.
frames.ask: Does the MAR hold an address, or a value?

frames.teach: Its partner, the memory data register (MDR), holds the data itself going to or coming from memory. So the MAR says which location, and the MDR carries the value there.
frames.ask:
From memory, name all
four registers you have now met.

frames.teach: How do these parts reach each other and memory? Over three shared sets of wires called buses. The address bus carries which location is wanted.
frames.ask:
Which register's contents would travel out on
the address bus?

frames.teach: (the address it is holding). The data bus carries the value itself, and the control bus carries the signals that say read or write, and when.
frames.ask:
Which of the three buses carries the value
itself?

frames.teach: Now the idea the examiner asks in a dozen disguises: architecture versus organization. Computer architecture is what the machine does, as the programmer sees it; it answers "what does the computer do?"
frames.ask:
Does architecture describe what the programmer can see, or the hidden
hardware?

frames.teach: Concretely, architecture is the instruction set architecture (ISA): the instructions available, the data types, the addressing modes, the registers a program can name, the instruction formats. Rule of thumb: if a program can see it or name it, it is architecture.
frames.ask:
So is the list
of addressing modes architecture?

frames.teach: (a program chooses among them, so architecture). Its opposite is computer organization: how the machine is built to do it. It is the hidden hardware, the control signals, the buses, the memory technology, the cache, how many execution units there are; the programmer never sees it, and it decides how fast the job gets done.
frames.ask:
Architecture answers "what"; organization answers which one-word
question?

frames.teach: Here is the clean test: can a program see it or name it? Then architecture. Is it an implementation choice hidden inside? Then organization. Try it on a hard one, the size of the cache.
frames.ask:
Is cache
size architecture or organization?

frames.teach: (a hidden build choice; no program names the cache size). Because the ISA is all a program sees, two chips with the same ISA run the same programs (they are binary compatible), yet can differ wildly in speed because their organization differs; that deeper hardware realisation is the microarchitecture.
frames.ask:
If two chips share an ISA, will one compiled program
run on both?

frames.teach: One hook to lock it in for the test: architecture is the blueprint (the design); organization is the construction (how it is actually built). Same blueprint, two builders, two speeds. (There are two whole ISA styles you will meet in Part C: the reduced instruction set computer, RISC, and the complex instruction set computer, CISC.) Now slide down to the sorting card below and read both columns; most arch-vs-org questions are simply "which side is this?"

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
Memorise these two lists. Most arch-vs-org MCQs are just "which side is this?"

Architecture (programmer-visible, "what")Organization (hidden build, "how")
Instruction set and instruction formatsControl signals and control-unit design
Addressing modesBuses and interconnection
Data types and their representationThe memory technology used
Registers a program can nameCache size and cache implementation
Whether floating-point instructions existNumber of cores and execution units, clock circuitry

Memory hook: architecture is the blueprint (the design); organization is the construction (how it is actually built). Same blueprint, two builders, two costs and two speeds.

blocks.label: The two component lists, and the books
blocks.html:
The lecture pauses twice to ask a question directly, and both come back as exam wording. Answer them now.

In-class questionThe answer, in the lecturer's words
What is the primary focus of computer architecture?The functional behaviour and logical design of the computer system
What does computer organization describe?The physical arrangement and implementation of hardware components

The example that settles every borderline case. Whether a computer will have a multiply instruction at all is an architectural issue. Whether that instruction is carried out by a dedicated multiply unit, or by a mechanism that uses the add unit over and over, is an organizational issue.

Two more of the lecturer's own examples

A smartphone: architecture defines its instruction set and data types, while organization determines its speed, battery life and multitasking.
Two laptops: both may be x86, the same architecture, yet differ in cache size, RAM speed and core count, which is organization, and so reach quite different performance.

A computer system is not a collection of hardware parts. It is a carefully designed system governed by both concepts together, which decide what it does AND how efficiently it does it. Understanding both is what lets engineers design better systems, programmers write optimised code, and organisations build high-performance computing solutions.

The two component lists, as the revision slide gives them.

Components of computer ARCHITECTUREComponents of computer ORGANIZATION
Instruction Set ArchitectureControl unit
Data types and representationALU unit
Instruction set and formatMemory organization
Addressing modesInput and output systems
Register setSystem buses and interconnections
System design, that is Von Neumann and HarvardPipelining and parallelism

Every row on the left is something a program can see or name. Every row on the right is a build choice hidden inside. That is the same test as the sorting card above, applied to six pairs at once.

The books, since the paper has named them. The first recommended text is Computer Organization and Architecture, 11th edition, by William Stallings, Pearson Education, 2019, one of the most widely used undergraduate textbooks on the subject. The others are Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface by Patterson and Hennessy, Structured Computer Organization by Tanenbaum, Essentials of Computer Organization and Architecture by Null and Lobur, and Computer Organization, Design, and Architecture by Shiva.

blocks.howto:
Same as before: keep the page covered, read a frame, do the small task, then
slide the card down one line to check.

frames.teach: Two ways to wire memory to the CPU, and the examiner wants the difference. The first you have already met, Von Neumann: one memory and one bus shared by both instructions and data. It is simple and cheap.
frames.ask:
In a Von Neumann
machine, how many memories hold the instructions and the data?

frames.teach: (shared). That single shared path has a price: the CPU cannot fetch an instruction and read data at the very same moment, they must take turns on the one bus. That traffic jam is the well-known bottleneck.
frames.ask: What do we call the slowdown caused by sharing one path?

frames.teach: The rival design is Harvard: separate memories and separate buses, one set for instructions and another for data. It costs more hardware, since the address, data and control lines are duplicated.
frames.ask: How many separate memories does a Harvard machine use?

frames.teach: That extra hardware buys one thing: Harvard can fetch an instruction and read data at the same time, a form of parallelism, and that is its whole advantage.
frames.ask:
Which design, Von Neumann or Harvard, can fetch an
instruction and read data at once?

frames.teach: So hold the trade in your head: Von Neumann is one memory, cheap but with a shared bottleneck; Harvard is two memories, more hardware but faster because both happen together. Now look just below at the two diagrams and the how to draw each note, and practise drawing both, because the paper asks for exactly that.

blocks.label: Draw it
blocks.tag: Von Neumann vs Harvard on paper
blocks.html:
How to draw each (the paper asks for a diagram, so practise it): draw the CPU as one box. For Von Neumann, join it by a single line, the shared bus, to one Memory box holding instructions and data together. For Harvard, draw two memory boxes, an instruction memory and a data memory, and join each to the CPU by its own bus.

How to remember it: Von Neumann = one box, one bus. Harvard = two boxes, two buses; picture the two upright strokes of the letter H as the two separate memories.

blocks.label: Von Neumann and Harvard, in the lecturer's own words
blocks.html:
The two diagrams above are the shape of it. Here are the details the paper asks for in prose.

What a Von Neumann processor consists of

A control unit, an arithmetic logic unit, a register set, and a memory region containing program instructions AND data.

That last item is the key feature distinguishing it from Harvard: a single area of memory for the program instructions and for the data those instructions act on.

Why it was designed that way. It is conceptually straightforward for programmers, and relatively easier for circuit designers, to put all the code and data a program needs in one memory region. Simplicity on both sides of the machine.

What strict Harvard does instead. It uses one address space and memory bus for program instructions and a separate address space and memory bus for data.

What Harvard buysWhat Harvard costs
Simultaneous access to instructions and data, which is a form of parallelismEssentially duplicating the address lines, the data lines and the control signals the processor must implement

Twice the wiring for the ability to do two things at once. Whether that is worth paying depends entirely on the job, which is why both designs are still in use.

Where each one is actually found

Von Neumann runs general-purpose computers, laptops and desktops. Its enhancements are cache memory, DDR memories, pre-fetching and processing in memory, all of which exist to soften the shared-bus bottleneck rather than remove it.

Harvard runs microcontrollers and embedded systems where faster access matters: the controller in a washing machine, or in a car.

Read that list of Von Neumann enhancements again. Cache, DDR and pre-fetching are the subject of the memory lesson later in this course, and every one of them is an answer to the bottleneck you met two frames ago.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Label each as architecture (A) or organization (O): (1) the list of addressing modes, (2) the size of the cache, (3) the number of general registers a program can use, (4) the technology the main memory is built from, (5) the control signals the control unit sends.
blocks.answer: 1 A (programmer names them), 2 O (hidden size choice), 3 A (programmer-visible), 4 O (implementation), 5 O (hidden). If you can explain why for each, you have this topic.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A bank upgrades its servers to processors with larger caches and faster RAM while keeping the same x86 instruction set. What has primarily changed?   (a) Architecture only   (b) Organization only   (c) Both   (d) Neither
blocks.answer: (b) Organization only. Same instruction set means the architecture is unchanged; larger caches and faster RAM are organization. This exact shape, "same ISA, faster hardware", appears again and again: the answer is always organization.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A developer runs the same compiled application on two processors from different manufacturers. This is possible because both implement the same:   (a) Instruction Set Architecture   (b) Microarchitecture   (c) Control unit design   (d) Cache hierarchy
blocks.answer: (a) Instruction Set Architecture. The same binary program runs on both because they share an ISA. Their microarchitecture, control unit and cache may all differ; that is organization, and it only changes speed, not what runs.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A processor fetches an instruction while simultaneously reading data from memory. Which architecture makes this possible?   (a) Stack   (b) CISC   (c) Von Neumann   (d) Harvard
blocks.answer: (d) Harvard. Separate instruction and data memories and buses let both happen at once. Von Neumann shares one path, so it cannot.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: When an MCQ says "same instruction set" or "same ISA" but the hardware changed, the change is organization, never architecture. And "which is visible to the programmer?" almost always points to the instruction formats / addressing modes / registers (architecture), not to caches, buses or memory technology (organization).

blocks.label: Every exam question on architecture, organization and the ISA

blocks.big:
"Architecture is the blueprint, what the machine does; organization is the
construction, how it does it."
blocks.sub: If a program can see or name it, it is architecture (the ISA); if it is a hidden build choice, it is organization. Same ISA runs the same programs. Von Neumann shares one memory; Harvard splits instructions and data so it fetches both at once.

title: Number Systems and Conversions
lead: Everything a computer holds is binary. This skill is turning numbers between binary, decimal and hexadecimal without thinking, plus the special decimal codes, and it is easy marks. We build it as a programme: many tiny steps worked through one at a time, and you check each one before the next. Go slowly and it will soon feel automatic.

blocks.label: Why a computer counts in twos at all
blocks.html:
Start with the wire. A computer is built of electronic circuitry, and information inside it is carried by currents, by voltage differences, or, for permanent storage, by the orientation of magnetic material.

Look at any one of those and ask what it can reliably tell you apart. Not a hundred voltage levels: noise would blur them. Two states, though, are unmistakable.

Key point

A single circuit or piece of magnetic material is regarded as being in one of two states, so it can represent a binary digit. That, and nothing more romantic, is why numbers are represented inside a computer in base 2.

Now the rule that makes any base work. A digit sequence an-1 ... a1 a0 stands for:

an-1 x basen-1  +  ...  +  a1 x base1  +  a0 x base0

Each digit is multiplied by the base raised to its column number, counting from zero at the right. Decimal already works this way and nobody thinks about it: 407 is 4 x 100 plus 0 x 10 plus 7 x 1. Change the base and nothing else changes.

What gets represented, and why it matters outside the exam. Data types and representation define how data is stored and interpreted:

  • integer formats, both signed and unsigned
  • floating-point representation
  • character encoding, such as ASCII and Unicode
Where it bites in real systemsWhy
Banking and financial softwareAccurate floating-point representation is critical. A rounding error repeated a million times is somebody's money
Multimedia, video and image processingRelies on data formats such as RGB encoding
Scientific computingSimulations need precision in floating-point calculations

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A base just means how many symbols you count with before you start a new column. Decimal is base 10: the ten symbols 0 to 9. A computer wire is only ever on or off.
frames.ask: So how many symbols does binary have?

frames.teach: (on or off), which is base 2. Binary is correct but gets very long, so we bundle it up as hexadecimal, base 16, whose symbols run 0 to 9 and then A, B, C, D, E, F.
frames.ask:
A is the first letter-symbol; what decimal
value does the hex digit A stand for?

frames.teach: Then B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15. Next, place value: reading a number from right to left, the columns are worth base0 = 1, then base1, then base2, and so on.
frames.ask:
In hex, what is the place
value of the third column from the right?

frames.teach: So the hex columns are 1, 16, 256, 4096. Three size words before we convert: one binary digit is a bit, four bits are a nibble, and eight bits are a byte.
frames.ask:
How many bits are in a
byte?

frames.teach: (and four bits are a nibble). Now the first conversion. To turn any base into decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add the results. Take the hex number 2F: its columns are 16 and 1, and F = 15.

That is every base-to-decimal question. The reverse, decimal to any base, divides repeatedly by the base, jots each remainder, and reads the remainders bottom to top. For 13 to binary: 13÷2 = 6 r 1, 6÷2 = 3 r 0, 3÷2 = 1 r 1, 1÷2 = 0 r 1.
frames.ask:
Read the four remainders
from the bottom up.

frames.teach: Let us prove it rather than trust it. The binary columns are 8, 4, 2, 1, and 1101 has 1-bits in the 8, 4 and 1 columns.
frames.ask: Add 8 + 4 + 1; do you land back on 13?

frames.teach: The conversion checks out. Now binary to hex. Because 16 = 24, one hex digit is exactly four bits, so group the bits into fours from the right and turn each four into one hex digit. Take 1101 0110: the right group 0110 = 4+2 = 6.
frames.ask: What hex digit is the left group 1101?

frames.teach:
(that is 8+4+1 = 13). So 1101 0110 = D6, and going the
other way you simply expand each hex digit back into its four bits.
frames.ask:
Read
on.

frames.teach: A few powers of two must be instant. 210 = 1024, which we call "1 K"; then 220 = 1 M and 230 = 1 G.
frames.ask:
How many bytes is
2<sup>10</sup>, and what one-letter name do we give it?

frames.teach: Every memory and cache question leans on these. Now the special decimal codes, where each decimal digit is kept on its own. First is BCD.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: BCD (binary coded decimal), the 8421 code, writes each decimal digit as its own 4 bits. So 59 becomes 5 = 0101 and 9 = 1001, written 0101 1001. It is a weighted code (the bit positions are worth 8, 4, 2, 1).
frames.ask:
Write the single
digit 7 in BCD.

frames.teach: (4+2+1 = 7). BCD is just the digit in plain 4-bit binary. The next code, Excess-3, takes the digit, adds 3, then writes the result in 4 bits. So 9 becomes 9+3 = 12 = 1100.
frames.ask: Write the digit 6 in Excess-3.

frames.teach: (6+3 = 9 = 1001); to decode you subtract 3. Excess-3 is non-weighted (its bits carry no fixed weight) and self-complementing.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Last, the character codes, which store text and not numbers. ASCII encodes English letters, digits and symbols in 7 or 8 bits; Unicode was introduced to cover the characters of all the world's languages.
frames.ask:
Which of the two would you
need for Chinese or Arabic letters?

frames.teach:
(it covers every language). That is every fact in
this skill. Now watch the moves used together in the two worked examples below, then sit the
recalls with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: The three conversions, and powers of two
blocks.html:
• Any base to decimal: multiply each digit by its place value and add. In hex the places are 1, 16, 256, 4096.
  • Decimal to any base: divide repeatedly by the base, write down each remainder, then read the remainders bottom to top.
  • Binary to hex: group the bits into fours from the right, turn each group of four into one hex digit. Hex to binary is the reverse: each hex digit becomes four bits. This works because 16 = 24, so one hex digit is exactly four bits.
n012345678910
2n12481632641282565121024

Memory hook: know these powers of two cold; 210 = 1024 = "1 K", then 220 = 1 M, 230 = 1 G. Every cache and memory question needs them.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.redo: Now redo it: the only hard part is remembering 4096, 256, 16, 1. Write those four first, then multiply.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.working:
1. Group in fours from the right: 1101  0110.
  2. Each group of four to one hex digit: 1101 = 8+4+1 = 13 = D; 0110 = 4+2 = 6.
  3. Write them in order: D6.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: go backwards too. 2A7F to binary is 2=0010, A=1010, 7=0111, F=1111, giving 0010101001111111.

blocks.label: The two conversions as algorithms
blocks.tag: the code the deck gives you
blocks.html:
You have done both conversions by hand. The deck also gives them as programs, and understanding the code is what makes the hand method impossible to forget.

Going TO a base: repeated division, building the answer right to left.

CaseWhat toBase does
n is zeroreturn "0"
n is negativeprefix a minus sign and recurse on the positive value
otherwiserepeatedly prepend toDigit(n modulo base), then divide n by the base

Prepend, not append. That is the code's way of saying "read the remainders bottom to top", which is the same instruction you follow on paper.

Its helper, toDigit, turns a value into a character: if n is less than 10 it returns n plus the character 0, and otherwise n plus the character a, minus 10. So 7 becomes the character 7, and 11 becomes the character b.

Going FROM a base: it is exactly evaluating a polynomial.

The method, and it is faster than place values

Process the digits left to right. Multiply what you have so far by the base, then add the next digit. Repeat to the end.

No powers, no place-value table, no risk of miscounting columns.

Watch it convert binary 1101 to decimal.

StepWorkingRunning total
start with 0, take the digit 10 x 2 + 11
next digit 11 x 2 + 13
next digit 03 x 2 + 06
next digit 16 x 2 + 113

So 1101 is 13 in decimal, which is the same 13 you converted the other way in the frames above. The two algorithms are inverses, and checking one against the other is a free proof.

The matching helper fromDigit maps a character back to a value: 0 to 9 give c minus the character 0; a to z give c minus a, plus 10, which allows bases up to 36; A to Z give c minus A, plus 10; and anything else throws an Invalid digit error. fromBase then strips a leading minus into a sign of -1, accumulates result = result x base + fromDigit(next character), and finally returns sign x result.

One liberating detail: the arithmetic inside a base conversion can be performed in any base you like. You do it in decimal because that is what your head is fluent in. A machine does it in binary. Both get the same answer, because the number never changed, only the way it is written down.

blocks.label: Hexadecimal in practice, and an error in the slides
blocks.tag: A34E, and the 6B5C that should be 6B5D
blocks.problem: Convert hexadecimal A34E to decimal and to binary. Then convert binary 110101101011101 to hexadecimal, and check the slide.
blocks.working:
Step 1: A34E to decimal, by place value

Four hex columns, worth 163, 162, 161, 160, that is 4096, 256, 16, 1. And A = 10, E = 14.

A34E = 10 x 4096 + 3 x 256 + 4 x 16 + 14= 40960 + 768 + 64 + 14 = 41806

Step 2: A34E to binary, which needs no arithmetic at all

One hex digit is exactly four bits, so take them one at a time: A = 1010, 3 = 0011, 4 = 0100, E = 1110.

A34E = 1010 0011 0100 1110

Step 3: 110101101011101 to hexadecimal, grouping from the RIGHT

Fifteen bits, so the leftmost group is short and gets padded.

110   1011   0101   1101
  • 110 = 6
  • 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11 = B
  • 0101 = 4 + 1 = 5
  • 1101 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 13
Now look carefully at that last group

13 in hexadecimal is D, not C. C is 12.

The slide groups the bits correctly, then labels the last group C and prints the answer 6B5C. The grouping it performed actually gives 6B5D.

Know both: the correct answer is 6B5D, and the slide says 6B5C. If that exact number appears on a paper, the printed key may carry the slide's value.

Step 4: shifting in hex, which is where the binary detour pays

A binary number is multiplied or divided by 2 by shifting the digits one place, left to multiply and right to divide. Hexadecimal cannot be shifted directly, so you decode, shift, and encode again.

StepValue
Start with hex3fc
Decode to binary0011 1111 1100
Shift right one place0001 1111 1110
Encode back to hex1fe

And 3fc is 1020 in decimal, 1fe is 510, which is exactly half. The check costs seconds and catches a mis-shift.
blocks.answer: A34E = 41806 = 1010 0011 0100 1110, and the binary groups to 6B5D
blocks.redo: Redo the grouping of 110101101011101 by first padding it to sixteen bits, 0110 1011 0101 1101. The groups are now unambiguous and give 6B5D again. Padding on the left costs nothing and removes the chance of mis-splitting a short leading group.

blocks.label: Binary Coded Decimal, and its three flavours
blocks.html:
Start with a digital clock. It never needs to show anything but the digits 0 to 9, one per position. Converting a whole binary number into decimal digits every second just to drive it would be wasted work.

So there is a code that stores each decimal digit separately.

Definition

Binary Coded Decimal is a type of binary code used to represent a given decimal number in an equivalent binary form, four bits per decimal digit.

Its main advantage is that it allows easy conversion to decimal digits for printing or display, and faster calculations. It is used for outputs that are always numeric, 0 to 9, such as digital clocks and digital voltmeters.

BCD is a WEIGHTED code, and that word carries the whole idea:

  1. Each binary digit in the four-bit group is assigned a weight.
  2. Add the weights of those bits whose value is 1.
  3. That sum is the decimal digit the group represents.

There are three different types of BCD, and the name IS the weights.

TypeWeights of the four bitsCode for 9.2
84218, 4, 2, 11001.0010
42214, 2, 2, 11111.0010
54215, 4, 2, 11100.0010

Check the 9 in each row and the weighting becomes obvious.

  • 8421: 1001 lights the 8 and the 1. 8 + 1 = 9
  • 4221: 1111 lights everything. 4 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 9
  • 5421: 1100 lights the 5 and the 4. 5 + 4 = 9

Three different bit patterns, all meaning nine, because the columns are worth different amounts. And the 2 after the point is 0010 in every row, since 2 is 2 under all three weightings.

8421 is the ordinary one, and if a question just says BCD it means 8421: the digit written in plain four-bit binary. The other two exist because different weightings make different arithmetic tricks possible.

blocks.label: Excess-3, the code that complements itself
blocks.html:
Excess-3, also written XS3, is a non-weighted code used to express decimal numbers. Non-weighted means the trick of adding column weights does not apply: you have to shift the value instead.

The rule, in two steps

Add 3 to each decimal digit, then write each new digit as four-bit binary.

That is all Excess-3 is, and the name says it: every digit is carried in excess of its true value by 3.

Work one. The XS3 code of 24:

DigitAdd 3Four-bit binary
250101
470111
24 in Excess-3 = 0101 0111

Three more from the deck, worth checking yourself:

  • 27 gives 0101 1010, that is 01011010
  • 597 gives 1000 1100 1010, that is 100011001010
  • 14.57 gives 0100 0111 . 1000 1010, that is 01000111.10001010

Why it exists at all. Excess-3 is particularly significant for arithmetic, because it overcomes the trouble 8421 BCD runs into when two decimal digits are added and the sum exceeds 9. Some old computers used it for exactly that reason.

Self-complementing, and this is the property examiners like

The 1's complement of an Excess-3 number is the Excess-3 code for the 9's complement of the decimal digit.

Watch it happen with 6.
Excess-3 of 6 is 6 + 3 = 9 = 1001
Flip every bit: 0110
0110 is 6, minus 3 = 3
And 3 is the 9's complement of 6, since 9 - 6 = 3.

So a hardware inverter, the cheapest circuit there is, performs a decimal 9's complement. That is the whole point of the code.

Coming back the other way. To convert Excess-3 to decimal: make groups of 4 bits starting from the radix point, then subtract 0011, that is 3, from each group.

StepValue
Excess-3 code1000110
Group and subtract 0011 from each00010011
Read the groups as decimal digits1 and 3
Answer13

One line to keep the two codes apart: BCD is the digit itself in four bits. Excess-3 is the digit plus three. If a code for 0 comes out as 0000 it is BCD; if it comes out as 0011 it is Excess-3.

blocks.label: Letters and symbols: the alphanumeric codes
blocks.html:
Start with what changed. Earlier computers were used only for calculation, as calculating devices and nothing else. Computers now hold names, addresses and item descriptions as readily as numbers.

But a computer is a digital system and can only deal with 1s and 0s. So to handle letters and symbols at all, it needs a code that turns them into numbers.

Definition

Alphanumeric codes, also called character codes, are binary codes used to represent alphanumeric data: letters of the alphabet, numbers, mathematical symbols and punctuation marks, written in a form a computer can understand and process.

They are also what lets you interface input and output devices, keyboards, monitors and printers, with the computer at all. A keypress is only useful if both sides agree which number means which letter.

The five to name. Morse code, Hollerith code, ASCII, EBCDIC and Unicode. The first two are historical, the middle two are examined in detail, and Unicode is the modern successor.

ASCIIEBCDIC
Stands forAmerican Standard Code for Information InterchangeExtended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
Width7-bit character code8-bit character encoding
Used onAlmost everythingMainly IBM mainframe and IBM midrange operating systems
Descended fromTeleprinter codesThe code used with punched cards, and the 6-bit binary-coded decimal code used with most IBM peripherals of the late 1950s and early 1960s

Inside the ASCII table, and the numbers are examinable.

  • Codes 32 to 127 are common to every variation of the table and are called the printable characters: letters, digits, punctuation and a few miscellaneous symbols.
  • Character 127 represents the command DEL.
  • Codes 128 to 255 are the extended ASCII codes. There are several different 8-bit variations, such as ISO 8859-1, also called ISO Latin-1.
  • Codes 129 to 159 hold the Microsoft Windows Latin-1 extended characters.
The one to hold on to

ASCII is 7 bits, EBCDIC is 8.
Seven bits give 128 codes, which is exactly why the ASCII table runs 0 to 127 and everything above it is called extended.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) Write decimal 255 in hex. (2) How many hex digits does a 20-bit binary number need? (3) A hex value shifted right by one bit is the same as which operation?
blocks.answer: (1) 255 = 15×16 + 15 = FF. (2) 20 ÷ 4 = 5 hex digits (one hex digit per four bits). (3) shifting right one bit is dividing by 2 (left one bit is times 2).

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) The Excess-3 code for decimal 9 is? (2) The Excess-3 code 0110 is which decimal digit? (3) The 8421 BCD of decimal 59 is?
blocks.answer: (1) 9 + 3 = 12 = 1100. (2) 0110 = 6, minus 3 = 3. (3) 5 = 0101, 9 = 1001, so 01011001. Remember: BCD is the digit itself in 4 bits; Excess-3 is the digit plus 3.

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Group binary into fours from the right, never the left, and pad the leftmost group with leading zeros if it is short. And do not confuse the codes: BCD is weighted (8421) and is just the digit in binary; Excess-3 is non-weighted and is the digit plus 3. "BCD" stands for binary coded decimal, nothing else.
