blocks.big: "Powers of the base, right to left. And four bits make one hex digit."
blocks.sub: To decimal: digit × place, then add. To another base: divide by the base, read the remainders bottom to top. BCD is the digit in 4 bits; Excess-3 is the digit plus 3.

title: Signed Numbers
lead: This is the most asked numeric topic, and the one most people find confusing. So we do it as a programme: many tiny steps, and you check each one before moving on. Go slowly. By the last frame the moves will feel obvious.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Start with 8 bits and no sign yet. The patterns run 0000 0000, 0000 0001, all the way up to 1111 1111. That top one, 1111 1111, is 28 − 1.
frames.ask: Write its value in decimal, then slide down.
So a top bit of 1 must mean what?

frames.teach: So just by glancing at 1010 1010 (top bit 1) you know it is a negative number. The only question left in the whole topic is which pattern to use for a given negative. The scheme real computers use is called two's complement, and the next few frames build it slowly.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Picture the 8 bits as a car odometer. It counts up 0000 0000, 0000 0001, and on to 1111 1111, then rolls back round to 0000 0000. Now turn it one step backwards from 0000 0000.
frames.ask: What pattern do you land on?

frames.teach: One step below zero. So it is natural to call 1111 1111 the value −1. Step back once more, to 1111 1110, and that is −2. Negatives are just the patterns you meet counting down from the top.
frames.ask: Counting back once more, what pattern is −3?

frames.teach: Counting all the way down would be slow, so here is the shortcut to build any negative: write the positive, flip every bit, then add 1. Try it on −1. Start with +1 = 0000 0001.
frames.ask: Flip every bit and write the result.

frames.teach: Now the second half of the shortcut.
frames.ask: Add 1 to 1111 1110. What do you get?

frames.teach: That is the same pattern the odometer gave for −1, so the shortcut is trustworthy. Say it like a chant: "flip every bit, add one." Now your turn, all by yourself: make −5 in 8 bits. Start with +5 = 0000 0101.
frames.ask: Flip, then add 1.

frames.teach: (0000 0101 flips to 1111 1010, and adding 1 gives 1111 1011.) That pattern is −5. Notice you only ever do three things: positive, flip, add one.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the other direction: reading a negative pattern back into a number. The trick is the very same one. Take 1111 1011 (top bit 1, so it is negative). Flip it and add 1 to find its size.
frames.ask: Flip 1111 1011, add 1, and say what size you get.

frames.teach: , so the value is −5. (Flip 1111 1011 to 0000 0100, add 1 to get 0000 0101.) Writing a negative and reading one use the same move, which is why it is worth learning well.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Why did the world settle on this scheme? Two reasons. It has only one zero (just 0000 0000), and the ordinary adder does subtraction for free, because a − b is the same as a + (−b). Here is the proof. Add −5 (1111 1011) to +5 (0000 0101), and drop any carry that falls off the top.
frames.ask: What 8-bit pattern is left?
Read on.

frames.teach: Last piece: the range. Half the patterns are negative and half positive, but zero uses up one positive slot, so there is always one more negative than positive: −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1. In 16 bits that is −32 768 to 32 767.
frames.ask: So in 8 bits the range is −128 to what?

frames.teach:
(−2<sup>7</sup> to 2<sup>7</sup> − 1 is
−128 to 127.) That is two's complement, start to finish.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Two older schemes you only need to recognise for the objective test. Sign-magnitude: a sign bit then the plain size, so −42 is 1 then 010 1010 = 1010 1010; its drawback is two zeros (+0 and −0). One's complement: negate by flipping every bit only (no add 1); it needs an end-around carry when adding and also has two zeros. Two's complement beat both by adding that 1.
frames.ask: How many zeros does sign-magnitude have?

frames.teach:
(+0 and −0). That is every idea in this topic.
Now watch all the moves used together in the worked example below, then sit it yourself with the
answer covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
• Write a negative: positive in n bits, flip every bit, add 1.
  • Read a negative (top bit 1): flip, add 1 for the size, then put a minus in front.
  • Add: add the patterns, drop any carry off the top (no end-around carry).
  • Range in n bits: −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1 (16 bits: −32 768 to 32 767).

Memory hook: one's complement is "flip"; two's complement is "flip and add one".

blocks.label: The four representations, and the first one that handles a minus sign
blocks.html:
Computers operate on binary values because they are built from transistors, and a transistor has two states. There are four commonly known integer representations, and the paper expects all four by name:

  1. Unsigned
  2. Sign magnitude
  3. One's complement
  4. Two's complement

Unsigned is the standard binary encoding and gives only positive values, with a range of 0 to 2n - 1. For four bits that is 0 to 15, since 24 - 1 = 15.

BinaryDecimalHex
101010a
110012c
111115f

But negative numbers are essential. A computer that could not deal with them would not be particularly useful, so three schemes exist to represent them: sign magnitude, one's complement and two's complement.

Sign magnitude: the obvious idea

Use one bit for the sign: 0 means positive, 1 means negative. The rest of the integer is a plain magnitude, encoded exactly as an unsigned integer would be.

It is how a human writes numbers, a sign followed by a size, which is why it is the first thing anyone invents.

Working with it is trivial in one direction. To get the additive inverse of a number you just flip the sign bit. In four bits, 0101 is 5 and 1101 is minus 5. So sign reversal and absolute value are easy operations in this scheme.

The method for a class exercise such as writing 74 and minus 43 in an 8-bit register: find the positive value in binary first, then flip the sign bit. The lecturer works minus 38 that way and gets 10100110.

The range is -(2n-1 - 1) to +(2n-1 - 1), so with four bits it runs from minus 7 to plus 7. Fifteen usable values out of sixteen patterns, and the sixteenth is the problem.

Three reasons it is not what real machines use

1. Two zeros. Because of the sign bit there are two representations for 0: 0000 and 1000, plus zero and minus zero. The hardware must make every calculation come out the same whichever one turns up, which costs circuitry.

2. Adding a negative is not subtracting. Adding the negative of a number is not the same as subtraction here, so separate operations have to be defined for add and for subtract.

3. It is slow. The hardware that does arithmetic on sign-magnitude integers is not fast, and it is more complex than the hardware for one's and two's complement.

Hold on to reason 2. Every later scheme is judged on whether one adder can do both jobs, and that is the whole reason two's complement won.

blocks.label: One's complement, and the carry that comes back round
blocks.html:
The second scheme drops the idea of a separate sign field entirely.

The rule, and it is one word

The one's complement form of a negative number is the bitwise NOT of its positive counterpart. Flip every bit. That is the whole of negation.

Positive integers use the same representation as unsigned, so nothing changes on that side. And like sign magnitude, it still has two representations of 0: 00000000 for plus zero and 11111111 for minus zero.

Two conversions worth working.

DirectionWorking
Write minus 4300101011 is 43. Flip every bit: 11010100, which is minus 43
Read 11100Top bit 1, so it is negative. Its additive inverse is 00011, which is plus 3 by sight. So 11100 is minus 3

The range is -(2N-1 - 1) to +(2N-1 - 1) with a plus and a minus zero, so a conventional 8-bit range is minus 127 to plus 127. The same range as sign magnitude, for the same reason: a wasted pattern.

The end-around carry, and why the scheme needs it

To add two one's complement numbers you do a conventional binary addition, and then an end-around carry: any carry that falls off the top is added back into the sum.

Watch it fail without the carry. Add minus 1, which is 11111110, to plus 2, which is 00000010.

StepResult
Binary addition alone00000000, which is wrong. Minus 1 plus 2 is 1, not 0
Add the carry back in00000001, which is correct

So the answer is only right after a second pass. That is an extra step in hardware on every single addition, and it is the second thing two's complement was invented to remove.

Where the name comes from. The negation of a positive value x can also be formed by subtracting x from the one's complement representation of zero, which is a long sequence of ones, that is minus 0. And a negative number's one's complement form can be obtained from its sign-magnitude form merely by bitwise complementing the magnitude.

It is not a museum piece for nothing: one's complement was used by real machines, including the PDP-1, the CDC 160 series and the UNIVAC 1100/2200 series.

blocks.label: Two's complement, and the shortcut worth using
blocks.tag: it fixes both problems at once
blocks.html:
Line up what the first two schemes cost and the third one writes itself.

ProblemSign magnitudeOne's complementTwo's complement
Representations of zeroTwoTwoOne
Extra step when addingSeparate add and subtractEnd-around carryNone, drop the carry
Key point

Two's complement solves the problem of multiple representations of 0 AND the need for the end-around carry. One zero, one adder for both addition and subtraction. That is why virtually every modern computer uses it.

How it relates to the scheme before it. In two's complement, a negative number is represented by the bit pattern that is one greater, in an unsigned sense, than the one's complement of the positive value. Which is exactly the flip-and-add-one you met in the frames, said the other way round.

The quick method, faster than flip-and-add-one under pressure

Write down the positive binary number. Then, reading from the right:
1. copy the digits up to and including the first 1
2. invert everything after that

14 in 6 bits is 001110. Copy from the right up to the first 1: 10. Invert the rest, 0011 becomes 1100. Result: 110010, which is minus 14.

No carry to propagate, so no chance of a carry error. Check it against flip-and-add-one once and then trust it.

The 8-bit values the lecture gives, worth checking yourself:

Decimal8-bit two's complement
+2400011000
+12701111111
-3911011001
-9210100100
-12810000000

Notice +127 and -128. The range is lopsided by one because there is only one zero, which is precisely the pattern sign magnitude wasted.

Reading one back. Take 110011. The most significant bit is 1, so it must be negative. Take its one's complement: 001100. Add 1: 001101, which is plus 13. So 110011 is minus 13.

blocks.label: Overflow, and the questions the lecturer sets on all of this
blocks.html:
Definition

When a value cannot be represented in the number of bits allowed, we say an overflow has occurred. It happens while doing arithmetic operations.

Two ways it shows up.

CaseWhy it overflows
8 in 3-bit unsigned8 needs at least 4 bits, 1000
8 in 4-bit sign magnitude8 needs at least 5 bits, 01000, because one bit has gone to the sign

And in an addition. In 3-bit unsigned, 011 (which is 3) plus 110 (which is 6) gives 1 001, that is 9. Nine needs four bits, so the addition overflows and the register keeps only 001.

Overflow means the true answer is too big or too small for the range. It is not division by zero, and it is not a hardware fault.

The revision class groups the whole topic like this, and the grouping is worth copying into the exam as a plan:

GroupMembers
Unsigned numbersPlain binary, positives only
Signed numbersSign magnitude, one's complement with its end-around carry, and two's complement
Other representationsFloating point numbers, and graphics and objects

The questions actually set on this material. The mid-lecture quiz asks you to describe how negative integers are formed under all three schemes, to say what 111100111 represents in each of them, and to perform 47 + 35 in 2's complement using 6 bits, stating what value would end up in the register. The homework asks for minus 89 in all three schemes in an 8-bit register, the range of a 16-bit register under sign magnitude, the value of 10111011 in all three systems, and 23.5 in IEEE single precision expressed in hexadecimal.

Work 47 + 35 in 6 bits before you move on. Six bits reach only to +31, so the true answer of 82 cannot fit, and what lands in the register is an overflow. That is the point of the question.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Store −182, 487 and −1023 in a 16-bit two's-complement machine (binary and hex) and add (−182) + 487. The exam sets exactly this; you will sit it verbatim in the final mock at the back. Here is how you write it on paper, one move at a time.
blocks.working:
Given 16 bits, two's complement · −182, 487, −1023
Formula range = −215 to 215 − 1 · negative = flip the positive and add 1 · group 4 bits per hex digit
Range: -2¹⁵ to 2¹⁵ - 1  =  -32768 to 32767   (all three fit)

487  =  0000 0001 1110 0111  =  01E7

-182:  +182  =  0000 0000 1011 0110
     invert  =  1111 1111 0100 1001
        + 1  =  1111 1111 0100 1010  =  FF4A

-1023: +1023 =  0000 0011 1111 1111
     invert  =  1111 1100 0000 0000
        + 1  =  1111 1100 0000 0001  =  FC01

(-182) + 487:
     1111 1111 0100 1010
   + 0000 0001 1110 0111
   ---------------------
   1 0000 0001 0011 0001   drop the carry off the top
     0000 0001 0011 0001   =  256+32+16+1  =  305
blocks.redo: Now redo it: positive, invert, add 1, every time. Practise with −75 in 8 bits (answer 1011 0101).

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: In 8 bits: (1) what decimal is 1000 0000 in two's complement? (2) what is the two's complement of 0010 1100? (3) what decimal is 1010 1010 in sign-magnitude?

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) How many representations of zero in sign-magnitude? (2) Which scheme needs an end-around carry? (3) The one's-complement pattern 1110 0011 is which decimal? (4) Why is two's complement used?
blocks.answer: (1) two (+0 and −0). (2) one's complement. (3) top bit 1 so negative; flip 1110 0011 to 0001 1100 = 28, so −28. (4) simpler and faster hardware (one zero, and add and subtract share one circuit).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Reading a negative two's-complement pattern, do not just read the magnitude bits off; you must flip and add 1 first. Overflow means the true result is too big or too small for the range, not division by zero. And the end-around carry belongs to one's complement only; two's complement simply discards the top carry.

blocks.label: Every exam question on signed numbers and complements

blocks.big:
"Flip and add one, to write a negative and to read one. Add the patterns, throw
away the top carry."
blocks.sub: Range in n bits: −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1. One's complement is "flip"; two's complement is "flip and add one", which is why it has one zero and one adder for both add and subtract.

title: Floating Point, IEEE 754
lead: One 32-bit pattern has to hold both a tiny number like 0.0000001 and a huge one like 6 billion, and plain whole-number binary cannot stretch that far. The fix is a trick you already know from science class, but people find it fiddly, so we do it as a programme: many tiny steps, and you check each one before moving on. Go slowly. By the last frame the three fields will feel obvious, and both exam directions fall out of a single line.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Here is the whole problem in one line. You have one box, exactly 32 bits wide, and it must be able to write both a tiny number like 0.0000001 and a giant one like 6,000,000,000. Plain whole-number binary, the kind you have used so far, cannot reach both ends.
frames.ask: Can plain whole-number binary write both of those in 32 bits? Yes or no?

frames.teach: It runs out of room. But you already beat this same problem in decimal, in science class: to write 6,020,000 compactly you put it as 6.02 × 106. Hidden in that little form are three separate pieces of information.
frames.ask: Name the three pieces.

frames.check:
a sign (it is positive, +), a fraction (6.02), and an exponent
(6).
frames.teach: That is all scientific notation is. Floating point does exactly this, but in base 2: a sign, a fraction, and a power of 2 instead of 10. Nothing more is going on.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: So a floating-point number is stored as those same three pieces, now called three fields, written left to right: the sign (s), then the exponent (E), then the mantissa M (which is just the fraction, also called the significand).
frames.ask: Which of the three fields sits on the far left?

frames.teach: Now their sizes. Single precision is 32 bits, split as 1 sign bit, then 8 exponent bits.
frames.ask: That leaves how many bits for the mantissa, to reach 32?

frames.teach: (1 + 8 + 23 = 32.) You only need to recognise the bigger size: double precision is 64 bits, split 1 + 11 + 52. Everything from here uses single precision.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: One preparation step, called normalising. In decimal you insist on exactly one non-zero digit before the point (6.02, never 60.2 or 0.602). In binary you do the same: slide the point until the number reads 1.something × 2e. Since the only non-zero binary digit there can be is 1,
frames.ask:
what single thing does a normalised
binary number always start with?

frames.teach: Always. And here is the first trick that helps: because it is always "1.", actually storing that 1 would waste a bit on something you already know for certain. So it is left out and just assumed. This is the famous hidden 1.
frames.ask:
When you READ a stored pattern back, what must you put in front of
the mantissa?

frames.teach: Put the hidden 1 back before you read. And going the other way, when you write a number you drop that leading 1 and keep only what follows the point. It costs nothing and buys you one extra bit of precision for free.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the second trick, the one that trips up most beginners: the bias. The exponent can be negative (for a tiny number like 2−3) or positive (for a big one). Rather than give the exponent its own sign bit, we add a fixed number, the bias, so the stored exponent is always a positive count. The bias is 127 for single (1023 for double). It is like storing temperatures as "degrees above −127", so a minus sign is never needed.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: So the stored exponent field is the true exponent plus 127. To undo that and get the true exponent back, you simply subtract the bias again. Suppose a pattern has an exponent field of 130.
frames.ask: What is its true exponent?

frames.teach: (130 − 127 = 3.) That is the whole method on one line, so learn it: value = ± 1.M × 2(exponent field − 127). Both exam directions fall straight out of it.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: One last reading skill: turning the mantissa into a number. After the hidden "1.", each mantissa bit is a smaller and smaller fraction: the first bit is worth 1/2, the next 1/4, the next 1/8. So a stored mantissa of 100… reads as 1.1 in binary, which is 1 + 1/2.
frames.ask: What is 1 + 1/2 in decimal?

frames.teach: Now decode a whole real pattern, one field at a time. Take sign bit 1, exponent field 130, mantissa 100…. The sign bit 1 means negative, the field 130 gives e = 3 (you just did that), and the mantissa gives 1.M = 1.5. First the power:
frames.ask: what is 2<sup>3</sup>?

frames.teach: Now hang the sign and the mantissa on it: value = −1.5 × 23 = −1.5 × 8.
frames.ask: Finish it: what number is that?

frames.teach: You just decoded a floating-point pattern by hand. Now prove the bias to yourself: to STORE that same exponent of 3 you would go the other way and do 3 + 127.
frames.ask: What exponent field would you store?

frames.teach:
The very field you started from, so the bias undoes
itself cleanly, going in and coming out. That is every idea in the topic: three fields, normalise to
1.something, hide the leading 1, and shift the exponent by the bias. Now watch all the moves used
together in the worked example below (it decodes this exact pattern, C1400000), then sit the two
"Your turn" boxes with the answer covered.

blocks.label: Scientific notation, and the three fields it needs
blocks.html:
Start with how you already write huge and tiny numbers.

Written outIn scientific notation
976,000,000,000,0009.76 x 1014
0.00000000000009769.76 x 10-14

The same three digits both times. Only the power changed. That is the trick: a range of very large and very small numbers can be represented with only a few digits, provided you also store where the point sits.

Key point

A number written as M x B±E can be stored in a binary word with three fields:
1. the mantissa M, the digits
2. the exponent E, the power
3. the base B, which is implicit and need not be stored at all

The base is always 2 on a binary machine, so storing it would waste bits on a number everybody already knows.

IEEE-754 and 854 is the standard for representing floating point, and the word floating is there because the decimal point can move. Fixed point nails the point in one place; floating point lets the exponent slide it wherever the number needs it.

This is what makes floating point useful for scientific calculation: one 32-bit format that reaches both very large integers and very small fractions, of the order of 10±38 in single precision.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
• Decimal to IEEE (single): (1) sign bit from the sign. (2) Convert the magnitude to binary. (3) Normalise to 1.something × 2e by moving the point. (4) Exponent field = e + 127, in 8 bits. (5) Mantissa = the "something" after the point, padded with zeros to 23 bits (the leading 1 is dropped, it is the hidden 1). (6) Put the 32 bits together and group in fours for hex.
  • IEEE (hex) to decimal: (1) write the 32 bits, split as 1 / 8 / 23. (2) Sign bit gives the sign. (3) Real exponent e = exponent field − 127. (4) Value = ± 1.M in binary × 2e (remember to put the hidden 1 back).

Memory hook: "sign, exponent, mantissa", and the exponent is always stored plus the bias, read minus the bias.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: Convert C1400000 (single precision) to decimal. This is the X the exam sets in Question 4a; you will sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given C1400000h, single precision
Formula value = (−1)sign × 1.M × 2(exp field − 127)
C1400000 = 1 10000010 100 0000...
  sign 1  ->  negative
  exp field 1000 0010 = 130,  e = 130 - 127 = 3
  mantissa 1.100... = 1 + 1/2 = 1.5
  value = -1.5 x 2³ = -1.5 x 8 = -12
blocks.redo: Now redo it: exponent field minus 127, then read 1.M as a binary fraction (first bit a half, next a quarter).

blocks.label: Putting 64.2 into IEEE single precision, all four steps
blocks.tag: the lecture example, including the repeating fraction
blocks.problem: Represent 64.2 in IEEE 754 single precision, and give the answer in hexadecimal.
blocks.working:
Step 1: get a binary representation, both sides of the point

The whole part is easy: 64 = 1000000. The fraction needs repeated doubling, which is the mirror of the repeated division you use for whole numbers.

Multiply by 2ResultBit taken
0.2 x 20.40
0.4 x 20.80
0.8 x 21.61
0.6 x 21.21
0.2 x 20.4 againback to the start

The pattern 0011 repeats forever. So:

64.2 = 1000000.0011001100110011...

Take each bit from the part that crosses 1, then drop the 1 and carry on. The moment a value repeats, so does the pattern, and 0.2 never terminates in binary. That single fact is behind most floating-point rounding surprises.

Step 2: normalise, so it looks like scientific notation

Move the point until exactly one 1 sits in front of it, counting how far you moved.

1.00000000110011... x 26

Step 3: bias the exponent

6 is the true exponent, and the standard stores it in biased-127 form.

6 + 127 = 133, and 133 in 8-bit unsigned is 1000 0101

Step 4: take the mantissa, and add the sign

The stored mantissa F is the 23 bits to the right of the point in the normalised form. The leading 1 is not stored; everyone knows it is there.

FieldValue
S0, since 64.2 is positive
E10000101
F00000000110011001100110

Now group all 32 bits in fours for hex

0 10000101 00000000110011001100110 = 42806666h
blocks.redo: Redo the four steps on 10.5, which is one of the exercises set: 10.5 is 1010.1, normalises to 1.0101 x 2 to the 3, so the exponent field is 3 + 127 = 130 = 10000010 and the mantissa is 0101 padded to 23 bits. The other exercises set are 9.999 x 10 to the 1 plus 1.610 x 10 to the minus 1, then 0.510 times minus 0.4375, and 1.10 x 10 to the 10 times 9.2 x 10 to the minus 5.

blocks.label: Overflow, underflow, and two disasters caused by them
blocks.html:
Both failures are about the exponent field running out of room, and the exam wants them apart.

WordMeaning
OverflowThe exponent is too large to be represented in the exponent field
UnderflowThe number is too small to be represented in the exponent field

Underflow, said more carefully: it occurs when the true result of a floating-point operation is smaller in magnitude, that is closer to zero, than the smallest value representable as a normal floating-point number in that datatype. It can in part be regarded as negative overflow of the exponent: if the exponent part can represent minus 127 to 127, then a result needing less than minus 127 may underflow.

The fix, and it is the one the exam wants

To reduce the chance of either, use 64-bit double-precision arithmetic. More exponent bits means a wider range before you run off either end.

What the standard demands. IEEE requires at a minimum the operations add, subtract, multiply, divide, remainder, square root and decimal-to-binary conversion, and it defines five exceptions: underflow, overflow, divide by 0, inexact and invalid.

Note that inexact is an exception in its own right. Most floating-point results are inexact, as 0.2 was above, which is why the standard treats it as a normal condition rather than an error.

Two failures that cost real money

Ariane 5, 4 June 1996. An unmanned rocket launched by the European Space Agency exploded forty seconds after lift-off on its first voyage, after a decade of development costing 7 billion dollars.
The cause was a software error: a 64-bit floating point number holding the rocket's horizontal velocity relative to the platform was converted to a 16-bit signed integer. The number was larger than the largest integer storable in 16 bits, so the conversion failed.

The Vancouver stock exchange, 1982. A new index was initialised at 1000.000 and updated after every transaction. Twenty two months later it read 520.
The cause: the updated value was truncated rather than rounded each time. Done properly, the index stood at 1098.892.

One is an overflow on conversion, the other is accumulated rounding error. Between them they are why this topic exists at all, and why an examiner asks you to name the exceptions.

Quiz 3 asks: the decimal value of BE7BAC10h read as IEEE single precision, and minus 82 in sign magnitude, one's complement and two's complement. The first is the decode method from the card above, run backwards.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Encode +6.0 in single precision. (Hint: 6 in binary is 110; normalise it.)

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) How many exponent bits in single precision? (2) The bias in double precision? (3) How many bits is double precision? (4) A floating-point number is stored as which order of fields?
blocks.answer: (1) 8. (2) 1023. (3) 64. (4) sign, then exponent, then mantissa (the exam phrases the answer as "sign, mantissa, exponent", meaning those three parts with the sign first; the true field order on the chip is sign, exponent, mantissa).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: Do not forget the bias: the exponent you compute is e + 127 going in, and field − 127 coming out. And the leading 1 is hidden, so when you read the mantissa put a "1." in front of it. Single precision has range about 10±38; double about 10±308.

blocks.label: Every exam question on floating point and IEEE 754

blocks.big:
"Sign, exponent, mantissa. Add the bias going in, take the bias coming out, and
always hide the leading 1."
blocks.sub: Single precision is 32 bits = 1 + 8 + 23, bias 127. One line runs both directions: value = ± 1.M × 2(field − 127).

title: Image and Memory Sizing
lead: A small, reliable question: how much memory a picture needs. One formula and a couple of unit facts, and the marks are yours. We build it as a programme of tiny steps, worked through one at a time, so cover the page and check yourself as you go.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A bitmap image (also called raster) is a grid of tiny squares, and each square stores its own colour as a few bits.
frames.ask:
So a bitmap picture is built
out of what?

frames.teach: A vector image is different: it stores the shapes as maths (lines and curves), so it can be scaled to any size with no loss of quality.
frames.ask:
A logo that must be blown up to billboard size with no blur, bitmap or
vector?

frames.teach:
(the maths redraws it crisply at any size). A
photograph, with its continuous shades, is stored as a bitmap.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now colour depth, the number of bits each pixel uses. Monochrome (black or white only) needs 1 bit per pixel; greyscale is often 8 bits; full colour is 24 bits.
frames.ask: How many bits per pixel does a monochrome image use?

frames.teach:
(only two states, black or white). Now the size
formula. The number of bits in a bitmap is width in pixels × height in pixels × bits per
pixel. Picture a small 100 by 50 pixel monochrome image.
To turn bits into bytes, divide by 8.

So the whole chain is pixels across ×
pixels down × bits per pixel, then ÷ 8 for bytes.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Often the size is given in inches at a certain dpi (dots per inch). Get the pixels first: pixels = inches × dpi, the same way for width and for height. Take 2 inches at 300 dpi.
frames.ask: How many pixels is 2 × 300?

frames.teach:
Do that for the width and the height, then feed
the two pixel counts into the size formula as before.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: One last caution. A megabyte can mean 1024 × 1024 bytes or a plain one million bytes, and the two give slightly different answers, so always say which you used. That is the whole skill. Now work the example below with the answer covered.

blocks.label: Bitmap against vector, and what each is good for
blocks.tag: two ways to store a picture
blocks.html:
Two types of graphics can be represented: vector graphics and bitmap graphics. They store completely different things, and the difference decides every question about them.

Bitmap stores the dots. Vector stores the instructions for drawing.

A bitmap remembers what colour each pixel is.
A vector image remembers what objects are there: a line, a rectangle, a circle, each with attributes that define it.

What a vector rectangle actually needs. To draw one you must store the start X and Y coordinates, the length, the breadth, the thickness and colour of the lines, the type of line such as dashed, and the fill colour. Eight small numbers, whatever size the rectangle ends up.

Vector, the draw packagesBitmap, the paint packages
Images can be enlarged without losing resolutionEach pixel can be altered individually
Objects can be edited by changing their attributesMore realistic for photos and real life
Objects can be layered in front or behind
Images take up less disc space

Which is why vector is ideal for drawing plans, working from a library of objects, and bitmap is what a camera produces.

Now the sizing calculation the lecture works. An image 4 inches by 6 inches at 300 dots per linear inch, black and white.

StepWorkingResult
Length in pixels6 x 3001800
Breadth in pixels4 x 3001200
Total pixels1800 x 12002,160,000
Bits, at 1 bit per pixelblack and white only2,160,000 bits
Bytesdivide by 8270,000 bytes
Kilobytesdivide by 1024263.4 KBytes

Watch the last step. Dividing by 1000 would give 270 KB, and by 1024 gives 263.4 KB. Both appear as options, so say which kilobyte you used, exactly as you must with megabytes in the worked example below.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: An image is 17.12 inches by 9.45 inches at 250 dpi, 1 bit per pixel. Find its memory in megabytes. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given 17.12 in × 9.45 in · 250 dpi · 1 bit per pixel
Formula pixels = inches × dpi (both ways) · bytes = pixels × bits / 8 · MB = bytes / 1024 / 1024
pixels across = 17.12 x 250 = 4280
pixels down   =  9.45 x 250 = 2362.5
total pixels  = 4280 x 2362.5 = 10 111 500
bytes = 10 111 500 / 8 = 1 263 937.5
MB    = 1 263 937.5 / 1024 / 1024 = 1.21 MB
blocks.answer:
10 111 500 pixels × 1 bit = 1 263 937.5 bytes ≈ 1.21 MB. Say
which megabyte you used (1024 twice gives 1.21; a million gives about 1.26).
blocks.redo: Now redo it: pixels first, times the bits per pixel, divide by 8, then by 1024 twice.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) How many bits per pixel for a monochrome bitmap? (2) A logo must be enlarged to billboard size without losing quality: bitmap or vector? (3) Photographs are best represented as?
blocks.answer: (1) 1 bit (two states). (2) vector (scales with no quality loss). (3) bitmap (a photo is a grid of continuous-tone pixels).

blocks.label: Every exam question on Von Neumann, Harvard and image data

blocks.big: "Pixels = inches × dpi. Bits = pixels × depth. Bytes = bits ÷ 8."
blocks.sub: For megabytes, divide by 1024 twice, and say which megabyte you used. Vector scales with no quality loss; a bitmap does not. Monochrome is 1 bit per pixel.

title: Instruction Sets and Formats
lead:
What a machine instruction is, the kinds there are, and the four
"address" formats the paper asks you to write a program in. Plus the counting question the
objective test likes.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: A machine instruction is one small command for the CPU. It always names an operation to carry out, for example ADD. The part that says which operation is called the opcode.
frames.ask: Name the part of an instruction that says which operation to do.

frames.teach: Sitting beside the opcode are zero or more operands: the things the operation works on. In ADD A, B the opcode is ADD, and A and B are the operands. (Each operand also carries an addressing mode saying where it is; that is the next section.)
frames.ask: In ADD A, B, what are A and B called?

frames.teach: Opcode and operands are just bit fields packed side by side. The fixed layout of those fields is the instruction format.
frames.ask: What word means the layout of the bit fields in an instruction?

frames.teach: (the instruction format). And the whole collection of instructions one CPU understands is called its instruction set. That is the vocabulary. Now the kinds of instructions.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: There are four main types. First, data transfer: LOAD, STORE, MOVE. These move data between registers and memory, and a LOAD in particular reads from memory into the CPU.
frames.ask: Does LOAD read from memory, or write to it?

frames.teach: Second, arithmetic and logic: ADD, SUB, AND, OR. This is the ALU's work. Third, input/output: talk to devices.
frames.ask: Which unit does the ADD and AND work?
Which type changes the order instructions run in?

frames.teach: Now the four address formats. This is only a count: how many operand addresses each instruction names. We go from most to fewest.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Three-address names both sources and the destination in one instruction, e.g. ADD X, A, B meaning X = A + B. Because each instruction does so much, you need the fewest of them.
frames.ask: How many addresses does ADD X, A, B name?

frames.teach: Two-address drops the separate destination; the destination doubles as one source, e.g. ADD A, B means A = A + B.
frames.ask: After ADD A, B, where has the result gone?

frames.teach: One-address works through a single register called the accumulator: LOAD a value in, do the operation, then STORE the result out. Only one address is named each time.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Zero-address names no address at all. It is a stack machine: you PUSH operands onto the stack, and ADD simply pops the top two and pushes their sum.
frames.ask: Which of the four formats is the stack machine?

frames.teach: Now the trade-off across all four. Fewer addresses means each instruction is shorter, but you need more of them.
frames.ask: Which format gives the shortest program (fewest instructions)?

frames.teach: And the other end: zero-address gives the longest program (most instructions), though each one is tiny. You will write one expression in all four formats in the worked example below.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach:
Now the counting question the objective test likes. To size a program in bytes,
count each instruction and add up, using: bytes per instruction = opcode bytes + (number of
addresses × bytes per address).
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: A single instruction's total length is just its fields added together. Take an 8-bit opcode, a 6-bit register field and an 18-bit address field.
frames.ask: Add them; what is the total length in bits?

frames.teach: (8 + 6 + 18 = 32.) When every instruction is the same size it is called fixed-length; these decode faster and are used by RISC. Variable-length instructions are used by CISC.
frames.ask: Which style, fixed or variable, is faster to decode?

frames.teach: Last one: to fit more opcodes into the same instruction length, you give the opcode more bits (and the operands fewer). That is every idea here. Now watch one expression written in all four formats in the worked example below, then sit the recall with the answer covered.

blocks.label: The ISA is the contract between software and hardware
blocks.html:
Start with a question you already know the answer to. Why will an app downloaded for your phone not simply run on a desktop PC, even though both are computers with a CPU, memory and storage?

Because the two processors do not speak the same language of instructions. That language has a name.

Key point

The Instruction Set Architecture, the ISA, is the core of computer architecture and acts as the interface between hardware and software. It is the bridge that lets a software program talk to the processor at all.

Being an interface, it has to state exactly what both sides can rely on. The ISA defines:

  • the set of instructions the processor can execute
  • the instruction formats, such as ADD, LOAD and STORE
  • the data types, such as integer and floating point
  • the registers available
  • the addressing modes

Or, said the other way round, it specifies what operations a processor can perform (the instruction set), how instructions are represented (the instruction format), and how data is accessed and manipulated (the addressing modes).

Three consequences the exam asks about directly.

ConsequenceThe example the lecturer gives
Applications compiled for one ISA only run on processors supporting that ISAMobile apps are built for the ARM-based processors in smartphones, which is why they are not desktop programs
An operating system is designed for a specific ISAWindows is optimised for x86 architecture systems
Different organizations, meaning different hardware implementations, can support the same ISA but vary in performanceTwo x86 chips run the same programs at quite different speeds

That third row is the arch-versus-org rule from Part A wearing its practical clothes, and the introduction deck states it twice because so many questions turn on it.

blocks.label: The five components of an ISA
blocks.html:
Every ISA is built from the same five parts. Learn the list, because a question that asks "which of these is NOT part of the ISA" is asking whether you have it.

ComponentWhat it isThe examples to quote
Instruction setThe complete set of instructions a processor can executeArithmetic ADD, SUB; logical AND, OR; control JUMP, CALL; data transfer LOAD, STORE
RegistersSmall, fast storage locations inside the CPUTwo types: General Purpose registers, and Special registers such as PC, IR, MAR and MDR
Data typesThe types of data supportedInteger, floating point, character, Boolean
Addressing modesThe methods used to access operands at runtimeImmediate, direct, indirect, register, indexed
Instruction formatThe structure of an instructionOpcode, operand or operands, addressing mode
Take one instruction apart

ADD R1, R2 adds R1 and R2 and stores the result back in R1.
The opcode is ADD. The operands are R1 and R2.
That is the whole of instruction format on one line, and every longer instruction is the same idea with more fields.

Notice the four instruction categories in the first row: arithmetic, logical, control and data transfer. They are the same four types the frames above worked through, and they come back in the next section with the lecturer's own processor examples.

blocks.label: Data movement: load and store
blocks.html:
Instruction types define the various operations a processor can perform on data. Between them they decide how a program moves data, performs computations, makes decisions, and interacts with memory and I/O devices. Each type handles one category of task, and together they form the complete functional capability of a CPU, which is why knowing them matters for writing efficient assembly, designing compilers and optimising performance.

Start with the first type: moving data about.

Load and store operations move data between a register in the processor and a memory location, or another register. Collectively they are called data movement instructions.

The two words are constantly confused, so fix them now

LOAD: the processor copies data INTO a register. Memory to CPU.
STORE: the processor copies data FROM a register into a memory location. CPU to memory.

Take the CPU's point of view and it reads itself: you load something into your hands, you store it back on the shelf.

The universal characteristic of instruction execution

The source does not get changed. Only the destination does.
Copy, never move. After LOAD the memory location still holds its value; after ADD the source operand is untouched. This one sentence is stated as a universal rule and is worth a mark on its own.

Every data movement instruction must therefore carry information identifying the source and the destination. If it named only one, there would be nothing to say where the copy is going.

The processor examples the lecturer names, and the exam quotes.

ProcessorInstructionsWhat is distinctive
MC68009LDA, STA, LDB, STB, LDD, STDThe direction is baked into the name: LD is load, ST is store, and the last letter names the register
MC68000MOVE, MOVEM, EXGMOVE works in either direction. MOVEM moves the contents of several registers into or out of memory in a single instruction. EXG exchanges register contents

Read the MC68009 names as two letters plus a register: LD-A loads accumulator A, ST-B stores accumulator B, LD-D loads the double accumulator D. Once you see the pattern you can generate the whole list rather than memorising six names.

blocks.label: Arithmetic and logic, then test and branch
blocks.html:
Arithmetic and logic operations provide the primary data-processing capabilities of the computer. This is the ALU's work, and the requirements are modest:

  • The minimum arithmetic operations required are addition and subtraction. Everything else can be built from those.
  • All processors implement the basic logic operations AND, OR and exclusive-OR, applied bit by bit between two operands.
The constraint on small processors, and it is examined

With operations needing two operands, smaller microprocessors usually require that one operand must already be in a destination register, while the other may be in another register or in memory.

Such processors may identify at most a single operand in memory. So they can ADD or AND to processor registers, but not to memory locations.

Compare the two instruction sets and the constraint becomes visible.

ProcessorTwo-operand instructionsThe rule that goes with them
MC6809ADDB, SUBA, SUBD, ANDA, EORA (EOR is exclusive-OR)Each one requires an operand to be in an accumulator. The last letter of the name says which
MC68000ADD, AND, OR, SUB, EORAll must specify source and destination, and with a few exceptions either may be a register or a memory location, or one of each

The bigger processor is the freer one: the MC6809 forces an accumulator into every operation, the MC68000 does not. That is an ISA design choice, and it is exactly the kind of thing the arch-versus-org question calls architecture.

Now the decisions. Test and branch operations provide the decision-making capabilities in computer programs, and they always come in that order: test first, then branch on the result.

  1. The test is usually performed on the result of some prior arithmetic or logic operation.
  2. It determines whether that result was zero or non-zero, positive or negative, or some other binary choice involving bits in the condition code register.
  3. During execution the processor examines the appropriate condition code bits to find the result.
  4. Depending on what it finds, the processor may or may not branch to a remote location for its next instruction.
The four branch instructions to know by name
InstructionBranch if
BCCthe carry is cleared
BEQthe result is equal to 0
BMIthe result is minus, that is negative
BRAalways, an unconditional jump

Read them as abbreviations and they teach themselves: Branch Carry Clear, Branch EQual, Branch MInus, BRanch Always.

Notice that BRA tests nothing at all. It is the one branch that is not a decision, and that is precisely why an examiner likes putting it among the other three.

blocks.label: Inside an instruction: the fields, and how to read one off
blocks.html:
An instruction is usually a combination of an operation code and some way of specifying an operand, most commonly by its location or address in memory. The instruction format is the layout of the bits, so that 11100011111110000001110000 is nothing more mysterious than ADD R1, R2 once you know where the boundaries fall.

That layout is usually drawn as a rectangular box standing for the bits as they appear in a memory word or a control register, divided into groups called fields.

The three most common fields, and what each does
FieldWhat it specifies
OpcodeThe operation to be performed
ModeThe way the operand, or the effective address, is determined
Address or OperandA memory address or a processor register

Now read a real one, 16 bits wide. The format is 4-bit opcode, 4-bit register, 8-bit address: the opcode names the operation such as ADD or SUB, the register field names a register such as R1 or R2, and the address gives a memory location.

BitsFieldMeaning
1010OpcodeADD
0011RegisterR3
11001010Address202
1010 0011 11001010  means  ADD R3, [202]

And a 32-bit, three-register one. The fields are 6-bit opcode then three 5-bit register numbers, with the rest unused.

BitsFieldMeaning
000001OpcodeADD
00001RegisterR1, the destination
00010RegisterR2, operand 1
00011RegisterR3, operand 2
00000000000Unusedpadding to 32 bits
000001 00001 00010 00011 00000000000  means  ADD R1, R2, R3

The method is always the same: know the field widths, split the bit string at those boundaries, then translate each group. The revision class repeats exactly this, that instructions divide into opcode, operands and addressing mode, that they typically carry 0, 1, 2 or 3 operands, and that there is usually more than one instruction format in an instruction set.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
bytes per instruction = opcode bytes + (number of addresses × bytes per address)

A single instruction's total length is its fields added: an 8-bit opcode + a 6-bit register field + an 18-bit address field = 32 bits. Fixed-length (all one size) decodes faster and is used by RISC; variable-length by CISC. More opcodes in the same length means giving the opcode more bits.

blocks.label: The four formats as the lecturer writes them
blocks.tag: X = (A + B) x (C + D), and what each format costs
blocks.problem: Write X = (A + B) x (C + D) in three-address, two-address, one-address and zero-address form, and say what each format costs.
blocks.working:
The whole topic is studied through this one assembly program, so learn the four versions as a set. Throughout, M[A] means the operand at the memory address symbolised by A.

Three-address

ADD R1, A, B
ADD R2, C, D
MUL X, R1, R2
AdvantageDisadvantage
Short programs when evaluating arithmetic expressionsThe binary-coded instructions require too many bits to specify three addresses

Two-address, which is the most common in commercial computers. Each address field can specify either a processor register or a memory word.

MOV R1, A
ADD R1, B
MOV R2, C
ADD R2, D
MUL R1, R2
MOV X, R1

MOV transfers operands to and from memory and processor registers. And note the rule that makes the format work: the first symbol listed is assumed to be both a source and the destination where the result is put back.

One-address, which uses an implied accumulator, AC, for all data manipulation. For multiplication and division a second register is needed.

LOAD A
ADD B
STORE T
LOAD C
ADD D
MUL T
STORE X

Every operation here is between the AC and a memory operand, and T is a temporary memory location holding the intermediate result. That is why the program grew: values must be parked in memory between steps.

Zero-address, on a stack machine.

PUSH A
PUSH B
ADD
PUSH C
PUSH D
ADD
MUL
POP X
Why it is called zero-address

Look at ADD and MUL: neither names an address at all. They take their operands from the top of stack, TOS, and put the result back there.

Only PUSH and POP need an address field, because only they communicate with memory. The name comes from the absence of an address field in the computational instructions.

One practical consequence: to evaluate an arithmetic expression on a stack computer you must first convert the expression into reverse Polish notation. The stack program above is exactly A B + C D + x read in that order.
blocks.answer: Three-address is the shortest program but the widest instructions; zero-address has the narrowest instructions but the longest program.
blocks.redo: The revision exercise sets the same task on a harder expression for a Pentium 4: X = ((A x B) + C/D) all divided by (F x G + J x K). The three-address answer runs MUL R1, A, B then DIV R2, C, D then ADD R1, R1, R2 then MUL R2, F, G then MUL R3, J, K then ADD R2, R2, R3 then DIV X, R2, R3. The zero-address answer begins PUSH A, PUSH B, MUL, PUSH C, PUSH D, DIV, ADD and ends with POP X. Write out the two-address and one-address versions yourself, then check that each still computes the same value.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.working:
The same expression in each format. Watch the instruction count climb as the number of addresses drops.

Three-address (shortest, 3 instructions):

ADD  T, A, B      ; T = A + B
ADD  X, C, D      ; X = C + D
MUL  X, T, X      ; X = T * X

Two-address (destination is also a source):

MOV  T, A
ADD  T, B         ; T = A + B
MOV  X, C
ADD  X, D         ; X = C + D
MUL  X, T         ; X = X * T

One-address (one accumulator, AC):

LOAD  A
ADD   B           ; AC = A + B
STORE T
LOAD  C
ADD   D           ; AC = C + D
MUL   T           ; AC = AC * T
STORE X

Zero-address (stack, most instructions but each is tiny):

PUSH A   PUSH B   ADD      ; A + B on the stack
PUSH C   PUSH D   ADD      ; C + D on the stack
MUL                       ; (A+B) * (C+D)
POP  X

The bigger version, X = ((A×B) + C/D) / (F×G + J×K), is Question 4b on the 2025/2026 paper and is in your final mock at the back.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) Which format is used by stack machines? (2) Which instruction category changes the program's execution sequence? (3) An instruction has an 8-bit opcode, a 6-bit register field and an 18-bit address field: total length? (4) Which is NOT defined by the ISA: addressing modes, instruction formats, internal ALU implementation, or visible registers?
blocks.answer: (1) zero-address (operands on the stack top). (2) control transfer (branch/jump/call). (3) 8 + 6 + 18 = 32 bits. (4) internal ALU implementation (that is organization, not the programmer-visible ISA).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: "Zero-address" goes with the stack and operands on top of the stack; do not mix it up with three-address (the shortest program). And the ISA defines what the programmer sees (formats, modes, registers), never how the ALU is wired inside.

blocks.big:
"Opcode says what; operands say what to. Fewer addresses, shorter instructions
but more of them."
blocks.sub:
Three-address is the shortest program; zero-address (a stack) the longest. Bytes =
opcode + (number of addresses × bytes each). Fixed-length decodes faster (RISC); variable-length
is CISC.

title: Addressing Modes
lead:
An address field in an instruction does not always hold the operand directly.
The addressing mode says how to turn that field into the real location, the effective address,
and then the operand. Learn the six or seven modes as "how many hops through memory", and this
is easy marks on both the paper and the objective test.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Here is the one idea behind every addressing mode. An instruction carries an address field, but that field does not always hold the operand you want. The mode is the rule for turning the field into the real place, and then the operand.
frames.ask: What does the addressing mode tell you how to find?

frames.check: the real location, then the operand.
frames.teach: Two names to fix first. The real location of the operand is the effective address, or EA. And M[x] is shorthand for "the value stored at address x", so M[1200] is the value sitting at address 1200.
frames.ask: In words, what does M[4500] mean?

frames.teach: We will grade every mode by one question: how many hops through memory does it take to reach the operand? We start with the fewest.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Immediate mode. The operand is a plain constant written inside the instruction itself, so you never touch memory to fetch it.
frames.ask: How many memory hops does immediate mode need?

frames.teach: Needing no memory access, immediate is the fastest way to supply a constant. Next, direct mode: the field is the address, so EA = the field and the operand = M[field], one hop into memory.
frames.ask: Direct mode reads memory how many times?

frames.teach: (one hop). Indirect mode adds one more hop. Now the field holds the address of the address: first EA = M[field], then the operand = M[ M[field] ]. That is two hops, a pointer to a pointer.
frames.ask: How many hops does indirect mode take?

frames.teach:
Because indirect follows an address that is itself
stored in memory, it is exactly what you need to chase pointers, for example down a linked list.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Two modes lean on a register instead of memory. Register mode: the operand sits in a named register, so no memory hop at all. Register indirect: the register holds an address, so the operand is M[register], one hop.
frames.ask:
In register-indirect, is the operand in the register, or at the address the
register holds?

frames.check: at the address the register holds.
frames.teach: Last group, the "add" modes; each adds something to the field to make the EA. Relative: EA = PC + field. Indexed: EA = index register + field. Base: EA = base register + displacement.
frames.ask: What does relative mode add to the field?

frames.teach: Now put it to work on one running example. Take PC = 7000, R1 = 1500, address field = 1200, and memory holds M[1200] = 4500, M[4500] = 999, M[1500] = 6000. Keep these in view. First, direct (EA = field, operand = M[field]).
frames.ask: Give the direct operand.

frames.teach: (EA = 1200, operand = M[1200] = 4500.) Now indirect on the same field: first EA = M[1200], then operand = M[that].
frames.ask: Work both hops and give the indirect operand.

frames.teach: (EA = M[1200] = 4500, then operand = M[4500] = 999.) Now register indirect with R1 = 1500: the register holds the address, so operand = M[R1].
frames.ask: Give the register-indirect operand.

frames.teach: (R1 = 1500, so operand = M[1500] = 6000.) Finally relative, an add-mode: EA = PC + field, with PC = 7000 and field = 1200.
frames.ask: Give the relative EA.

frames.teach:
(7000 + 1200 = 8200. The table gives no M[8200], so
you would report the EA and never invent a value.)
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the whole thing on one card. Immediate = the operand is in the instruction (zero hops). Direct = one hop. Indirect = two hops. And the add-modes (relative, indexed, base) add a register or the PC to the field first, then read there.
frames.ask: Order these by hops, fewest first: direct, immediate, indirect.

frames.teach:
That is every mode
you need. Now study the worked example and recall below, which run this exact PC = 7000, R1 = 1500,
field = 1200 example, and sit them with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
The effective address (EA) is where the operand really is; M[x] means "the value stored at address x". Each mode is one more hop than the last:

ModeEffective addressOperand is
Immediatenonethe value inside the instruction (a constant)
DirectEA = the address fieldM[address field]
IndirectEA = M[address field]M[ M[address field] ]
Registernonethe value in the named register
Register indirectEA = contents of the registerM[register]
Relative (PC-relative)EA = PC + address fieldM[PC + field]
IndexedEA = index register + address fieldM[index + field]
BaseEA = base register + displacementM[base + displacement]

Memory hook: immediate = in the instruction (zero hops, fewest memory accesses); direct = one hop; indirect = two hops (a pointer to a pointer). Register indirect uses a register as the pointer; relative, indexed and base all add something to the field.

blocks.label: Each mode, step by step, with the lecturer's own examples
blocks.html:
The card above gives the modes as a table. Here is what the CPU actually does in each, because the exam asks for the steps in words as often as it asks for a number.

Immediate: zero hops

One of the simplest and fastest modes in the whole ISA. The actual operand, the data value itself, is directly embedded inside the instruction, rather than sitting in a register or in memory.

Nothing is fetched, so nothing can be slow. That is the whole advantage.

Direct: one hop, in four steps. The address field contains the actual memory location of the operand.

  1. The CPU reads the instruction.
  2. It extracts the memory address from the address field.
  3. It accesses that memory location.
  4. It retrieves or stores the data.

Indirect: two hops. Here the address field contains the address of another memory location, and it is that second location which stores the effective address of the operand. The instruction format is simply Opcode then Address, but the address field is a pointer to the operand's address, not to the operand.

  1. The CPU fetches the instruction.
  2. It reads the address field A.
  3. It goes to memory location A.
  4. It retrieves the effective address stored there.
  5. It accesses the operand using that effective address.

Four worked indirect examples, and they are worth doing on paper.

InstructionMemoryResult
LOAD R1, (200)M[200] = 500, M[500] = the dataR1 = M[500]
LOAD R2, (300)M[300] = 400, M[400] = 50R2 = 50
ADD R1, (150)R1 = 10, M[150] = 250, M[250] = 5R1 = 10 + 5 = 15
STORE R3, (500)R3 = 30, M[500] = 800M[800] becomes 30

Notice the last one. On a STORE the two hops still happen, but the second one is where the value goes, not where it comes from. M[500] is untouched; M[800] changes.

Relative: the PC does the work

Effective Address = PC + Offset.

1. The CPU fetches the instruction.
2. The PC already points at the next instruction.
3. The offset is extracted and added to the PC.
4. The result is the target address.

InstructionPCEffective addressMeaning
BEQ R1, R2, +30200200 + 30 = 230Jump to 230 if R1 equals R2
BNE R3, R4, -4010001000 - 40 = 960Jump to 960 if R3 does not equal R4

The offset is signed, which is what lets a loop jump backwards. That is the entire reason branches use this mode rather than direct addressing.

Contents1200450060008100999200400

Why any of this matters outside the paper: compilers choose addressing modes to optimise speed; embedded systems need efficient memory access because memory is scarce; and in gaming systems fast memory access is what holds up the frame rate.

title: CPU Performance
lead:
How fast a processor runs is a calculation, not a mystery. Two formulas do
almost everything: the CPU-time equation and Amdahl's law. This is the most heavily weighted
numeric topic on the recent paper.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Everything about processor speed comes from one equation. A program's running time is three numbers multiplied together: CPU time = IC × CPI × T. IC is the instruction count (how many instructions actually run), CPI is the average cycles per instruction, and T is how long one clock cycle lasts.
frames.ask: Say what each of the three, IC, CPI and T, stands for, then slide down.

frames.check: instruction count, average cycles per instruction, clock cycle time.
frames.teach: The clock rate you see advertised (say 4 GHz) is cycles per second, so one cycle lasts T = 1 / clock rate.
frames.ask: Put that in place of T and write CPU time using clock rate.

frames.teach: So a faster clock shortens the time, but a smaller instruction count or a smaller CPI does too. All three matter.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Look closer at CPI. Instructions are not all equal: a register add may take 1 cycle, an indirect memory access 4. The average CPI weights each type by how often it appears, adding up (fraction of the type × its cycles) over all types. The fractions must add to 1.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Try a tiny one. A program is 70% simple instructions at 1 cycle each and 30% at 3 cycles each.
frames.ask: Work out the average CPI: (0.70 × 1) + (0.30 × 3).

frames.teach: (0.70 × 1 = 0.70, and 0.30 × 3 = 0.90, giving 1.60.) Notice 0.70 and 0.30 add to 1, exactly as the fractions must.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: A second speed measure is MIPS, millions of instructions per second: MIPS = clock rate / (CPI × 10<sup>6</sup>). A faster clock or a lower CPI both raise it.
frames.ask: If the clock rate is 2 × 10<sup>9</sup> and CPI is 2, find the MIPS.

frames.teach: (2 × 10<sup>9</sup> divided by (2 × 10<sup>6</sup>) gives 1000.)
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: When you improve something, always measure the gain against the OLD time: improvement = (old − new) / old.
frames.ask: Old time 200, new time 150: what fraction is the improvement?

frames.teach: ((200 − 150) / 200 = 50 / 200 = 0.25.) Divide by the old value, never the new.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: So is a chip fast just because its clock is fast? No. Because time = (IC × CPI) / clock rate, the instruction count and CPI count just as much, and behind CPI sit cache behaviour, branch prediction and instruction-level parallelism.
frames.ask: Name one reason a high-clock chip can still be slow.

frames.teach: (or a large instruction count, or poor cache or branch behaviour). That is why "judge a processor by clock frequency only" is wrong.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the second big formula, Amdahl's law. Suppose you speed up only PART of a task. The part you did not touch still takes its full time, so it caps the gain. Let f be the fraction of the original time spent in the part you improve, and let s be how many times faster you make that part.
frames.ask: In your own words, what does f stand for?

frames.check: the fraction of the time spent in the part you speed up.
frames.teach: That part's time shrinks from f to f / s, while the rest, (1 − f), is unchanged. If the whole job was time 1, the new time is (1 − f) + f / s, and speedup is old over new.
frames.ask: Write the speedup S.

frames.teach: Old time 1 on top, new time (1 − f) + f / s on the bottom.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Push s as large as you like, so f / s shrinks towards 0. Then S climbs only as far as 1 / (1 − f), because the untouched (1 − f) never goes away. Memory hook: the slow part you left alone sets the ceiling.
frames.ask: With f = 0.85, what is the best speedup possible, even with an infinite s?

frames.teach: (1 / (1 − 0.85) = 1 / 0.15 = 6.67.) Now a real, finite case: a cache 10 times faster (s = 10) that the CPU hits 85% of the time (f = 0.85). First find the new time, (1 − f) + f / s.

frames.ask: Finish it: what is S?

frames.teach: (1 / 0.235 = 4.26.) Far below the cache's 10 times, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate, which is exactly Amdahl's point. The reference card and the two worked examples below sit both of these formulas; do them with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.tag: the performance formulas on one card
blocks.html:
• CPU time = IC × CPI × T = (IC × CPI) / clock rate (since T = 1 / clock rate).
  • Average CPI = Σ(fraction of each type × its cycles), and the fractions add to 1.
  • MIPS = clock rate / (CPI × 106).
  • Improvement = (old − new) / old, always against the old time.
  • Amdahl's law: S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f / s), ceiling 1 / (1 − f).

Memory hook: the slow part you left alone sets the ceiling, no matter how fast you make the rest.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: One million instructions, by addressing mode: Register 40% at 1 cycle, Immediate 20% at 1, Direct 15% at 2, Indirect 10% at 4, Indexed 10% at 3, Relative 5% at 2. Find the average CPI and total cycles; then optimise indirect to 2 cycles and give the improvement. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given IC = 1 000 000 · the share and cycle cost of each mode
Formula CPI = Σ(fraction × cycles) · total = IC × CPI · improvement = (old − new) / old
Avg CPI = 0.40x1 + 0.20x1 + 0.15x2 + 0.10x4 + 0.10x3 + 0.05x2
        = 0.40 + 0.20 + 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.30 + 0.10
        = 1.70

Total cycles = 1 000 000 x 1.70 = 1 700 000

Indirect 4 -> 2:  new CPI = 1.70 - 0.10x4 + 0.10x2
                          = 1.70 - 0.20
                          = 1.50

Improvement = (1.70 - 1.50) / 1.70 = 0.20 / 1.70 = 11.76%
blocks.answer: CPI 1.70; total cycles 1 700 000; new CPI 1.50; improvement 11.76%.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: weighted average, then recompute with the one changed cost.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: A cache is 10 times faster than main memory, and the CPU finds what it needs in cache 85% of the time. Find the overall speedup. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given f = 0.85 (cache hits) · s = 10
Formula S = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s)
S = 1 / ((1 - 0.85) + 0.85/10)
  = 1 / (0.15 + 0.085)
  = 1 / 0.235
  = 4.26
blocks.answer:
S = 4.26, far below 10, because the 15% of slow accesses dominate. That
is exactly Amdahl's point.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: the "10 times faster" is s, not the answer; only the 85% gets divided by s, the other 15% stays at full cost.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) A benchmark runs 12 billion instructions at 4 GHz with an average CPI of 1.5. Execution time? (2) Why should performance not be judged by clock frequency alone?
blocks.answer: (1) time = (IC × CPI) / clock rate = (12×109 × 1.5) / (4×109) = 18 / 4 = 4.5 seconds. (2) because it also depends on CPI, instruction count, cache behaviour and instruction-level parallelism, not clock speed by itself.

blocks.html: Improvement is measured against the old time, (old − new)/old, not the new. In Amdahl's law, f is the fraction sped up and only that part is divided by s; a "10 times faster" cache with 85% hits gives about 4.26, not 10.

the ceiling."
