title: Pipelining and Hazards
lead:
Overlapping instructions so several are in progress at once, like a laundry
that washes one load while drying the last. It speeds the processor up, and the paper asks you
to compute that speedup and to name the hazards that get in the way.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Pipelining means overlapping instructions so several are in progress at once. Picture a laundry: you do not wait for one load to wash, dry and fold before starting the next, because the moment the first load moves to the dryer the second goes into the washer. A processor overlaps its instructions the same way.
frames.ask: What everyday process is pipelining most like?

frames.teach: (or any assembly line). To overlap them, we split each instruction into stages, called k stages. A common five are IF (instruction fetch), ID (instruction decode), EX (execute), MEM (memory access) and WB (write back). Each stage is its own hardware, so five instructions can each sit in a different stage at the same moment.
frames.ask: Name the five stages in order.

frames.teach: Without a pipeline, instruction 2 cannot start until instruction 1 has passed through every stage. With a pipeline, the instant an instruction leaves a stage the next one enters it, so once the pipe is full one instruction finishes every clock cycle.
frames.ask: Once the pipe is full, how many instructions complete per clock cycle?

frames.teach: That steady one-per-cycle output is the whole payoff. Now, how long is one clock cycle? Every stage must finish inside it, so the cycle is set by the slowest stage plus a small latch delay between stages, never the average and never the sum.
frames.ask: If the stages take 60, 50, 90, 80 ns with a 10 ns latch, what is the cycle time?

frames.teach: (The slowest stage is 90 ns, plus the 10 ns latch, giving 100 ns.)
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the time for n instructions. The first takes k cycles to fill the pipe; after that one more finishes every cycle, so n instructions take (k + n − 1) cycles, which you then multiply by the cycle time.
frames.ask: With k = 4 stages and n = 500 tasks, how many cycles is that?
Read on.

frames.teach: Without the pipeline each instruction needs its full one-instruction time, the sum of the stage times, here 60 + 50 + 90 + 80 = 280 ns. The speedup is that one-instruction time divided by the cycle time, and it can never exceed k, the number of stages.
frames.ask: Divide 280 ns by the 100 ns cycle to get the speedup.

frames.teach: (280 / 100 = 2.8, below the ceiling of k = 4 stages.) For a whole batch you compare totals instead: 500 × 280 = 140 000 ns without a pipeline, against 50 300 ns with one. The reference card and the two worked examples below sit exactly these; do them with the answers covered.

blocks.label: What pipelining is, and the five stages by name
blocks.html:
The goal first. One of the major goals of computer architecture is to improve speed and overall performance without excessively increasing hardware cost. Pipelining is the answer that costs almost nothing: it does not add units, it just stops them standing idle.

Definition, three ways the lecture puts it

1. A performance enhancement technique in which multiple instructions are processed simultaneously by dividing instruction execution into several stages.
2. An implementation technique where arithmetic sub-operations, or the phases of the instruction cycle, overlap in execution.
3. Decomposing a sequential process into sub-operations, each executed in a dedicated segment that operates concurrently with all the others.

It exploits parallelism among instructions, which has a name worth quoting: Instruction Level Parallelism, ILP.

The picture is an automobile assembly line: many steps, stages or segments, each carrying out a different part of the operation, connected to form a pipe. An instruction enters at one end and progresses through the stages to exit at the other.

The five stages, and this list is examined by name.

StageWhat it does
IF, Instruction FetchRetrieves the instruction from memory, and increments the PC
ID, Instruction DecodeInterprets it: translates the opcode into control signals and reads the registers
EX, ExecutePerforms the decoded operation: the ALU work, and computing any jump or branch target
MEM, Memory AccessAccesses memory if required
WB, Write BackStores the result back into a register, updating the register file

That is the five-stage RISC load-store pipeline, and it is the same five in the RISC lesson. IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB. Say them in order until they come out as one word.

What it buys, and the vocabulary that goes with it

By letting different instructions occupy different stages simultaneously, pipelining increases the THROUGHPUT of the processor, so more instructions complete in less time.

Throughput is the number of items, cars or instructions, that exit the pipeline per unit time: 1 instruction per clock cycle, or 10 cars per hour.

The designer's goal is a balanced pipeline, meaning every stage takes about the same time. In general the stage time is the time per instruction on a non-pipelined machine divided by the number of stages, and in practice it is the maximum of all the stage times. A pipeline yields a reduction in cycles per instruction, with CPI roughly equal to the stage time.

Pipelining is one of several kinds of parallelism. Speedup in a real system comes from parallelism at all levels: multi-user, multitasking, multi-processing, multi-programming, multi-threading and compiler optimizations. And there are three types of pipeline to name: the instruction pipeline, the operation pipeline, and multi-issue pipelines.

What it costs. Pipelining introduces pipeline hazards, data dependencies, branch instructions and resource conflicts. Architects answer those with forwarding, stalling and branch prediction, all of which come later in this lesson. It is used by every modern processor, Intel and AMD included, because it improves CPU utilization, instruction throughput and overall speed.

blocks.label: Why overlapping wins, from the laundry to the algebra
blocks.tag: the analogies, then the formula they produce
blocks.problem: Ann, Brian, Cathy and Dave each have one load of washing. Washing, drying, folding and stashing take 30 minutes each. How long does it take done one at a time, and how long overlapped?
blocks.working:
Step 1: one at a time

one load = 30 min x 4 stages = 120 minutesfour loads = 4 x 120 = 480 minutes, that is 8 hours

Step 2: overlapped

The moment Ann's load leaves the washer, Brian's goes in. The machines never sit idle.

four loads overlapped = 3.5 hoursspeedup = 8 / 3.5 = 2.1
Four sentences that carry the whole topic

1. Pipelining does not help the latency of a single task. Ann still waits two hours.
2. It helps the throughput of the entire workload.
3. The rate is limited by the slowest stage.
4. The potential speedup equals the number of stages as the number of tasks grows. Unbalanced stage lengths reduce it, and so do the time to fill the pipe and the time to drain it.

Step 3: the same idea in a classroom. One hundred students sit an exam of five problems. Five markers each grade one problem only, passing each script on as soon as they finish their part. Each problem takes 12 minutes, so any one script still takes an hour, but all hundred are graded five times quicker. Latency unchanged, throughput multiplied.

Step 4: what it looks like in hardware. The key idea is to break a big computation into pieces and separate each piece with a pipeline register, so a 1 ns computation becomes five 200 ps stages. (A nanosecond is 10-9 s and a picosecond is 10-12 s.) In the load example each of the five stages has its own functional unit, used once, and the second load starts as soon as the first finishes its fetch. Each load still takes five cycles; the throughput is far higher. Comparing three lw instructions: the non-pipelined machine takes 800 ps per instruction, the pipelined one advances every 200 ps.

Step 5: now the algebra, which every numeric question uses. Let n be the number of tasks, k the number of stages, T the time per stage.

QuantityFormula
Time per taskT x k
Total, not pipelinedT x k x n, or n x tn where tn is the clock cycle
Total, pipelinedT x k + T x (n - 1), that is (k + n - 1) x tp
SpeedupSk = n x tn / ((k + n - 1) x tp), which is kn / (k + n - 1) and approaches k when n is far greater than k

Step 6: three worked cases from the deck.

Case A, a 4-stage pipeline, tp = 20 ns, 100 tasks. One task non-pipelined is 20 x 4 = 80 ns.

pipelined = (4 + 99) x 20 = 2060 ns    non-pipelined = 100 x 80 = 8000 nsspeedup = 8000 / 2060 = 3.88

Note it is 3.88 and not 4. A 4-stage pipeline is basically identical to a system with 4 identical functional units, so 4 is the ceiling, and the fill time keeps you just below it.

Case B, two designs compared. Design 1's average instruction time is clock cycle x CPI:

10 ns x (4 x 0.4 + 4 x 0.2 + 5 x 0.4) = 44 ns

Design 2 at steady state costs one clock cycle plus 1 ns for setup and clock skew, that is 11 ns, so the speedup is 44 / 11 = 4.

Case C, unequal stages. Functional units of 10, 8, 10, 10 and 7 ns with 1 ns overhead per stage.

pipelined stage time = max(10, 8, 10, 10, 7) + 1 = 11 nsnon-pipelined = 10 + 8 + 10 + 10 + 7 = 45 ns    speedup = 45 / 11 = 4.1 times

Look at what the 8 ns and 7 ns stages bought you: nothing. The clock runs at the slowest stage, so every fast stage simply waits. That is why a balanced pipeline is the designer's goal.
blocks.answer: 480 minutes sequential, 3.5 hours overlapped, a speedup of 2.1
blocks.redo: Redo the laundry with eight loads instead of four. Sequential is 960 minutes; overlapped is (4 + 8 - 1) x 30 = 330 minutes, a speedup of 2.9. Twelve loads give 3.3. The speedup climbs towards 4, the number of stages, and never reaches it, which is exactly what kn / (k + n - 1) says.

blocks.label: Efficiency and throughput
blocks.html:
Speedup is not the only measure the paper asks for. Two more, and both are ratios you can reason about rather than memorise.

MeasureDefinitionFormula
Efficiency, EThe ratio of the busy time span to the total time span including idle timeE = n / (m + n - 1)
Throughput, TThe number of results achieved per unit timeT = n / ((m + n - 1) x c) = E / c
Read the efficiency formula and it explains itself

E = n / (m + n - 1)

The top is the work done. The bottom is the cycles spent, including the m - 1 cycles wasted filling the pipe.

As n tends to infinity, E becomes 1: run enough tasks and the fill cost disappears into the average. Run one task and it is 1/m, the worst case.

Throughput denotes the computing power of the pipeline. It is efficiency divided by the cycle time, so it says results per second where efficiency says results per cycle.

Maximum speedup, maximum efficiency and maximum throughput are all ideal cases. They assume no hazards, perfectly balanced stages, and an endless stream of independent instructions. The next section is about all three of those assumptions failing.

blocks.label: Must do
blocks.html:
• Cycle time = slowest stage + latch delay.
  • Pipelined time for n tasks = (k + n − 1) × cycle time. (It takes k cycles to fill with the first task, then one more cycle for each of the other n − 1.)
  • Non-pipelined time for n tasks = n × (time for one instruction). One instruction takes the sum of all the stage times, or the given per-instruction time.
  • Speedup = non-pipelined time / pipelined time. Its ceiling is k.

Memory hook: "k + n − 1", and the clock runs at the slowest stage, never the average.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: A pipeline has 4 phases of 60, 50, 90, 80 ns, with a 10 ns latch delay. Find the cycle time, the one-task time, the speedup, and the times for 500 tasks. The exam sets exactly this; sit it verbatim in the final mock.
blocks.working:
Given 4 phases 60, 50, 90, 80 ns · latch 10 ns · 500 tasks
Formula cycle = slowest + latch · pipe(n) = (k + n − 1) × cycle · seq(n) = n × Σphases · speedup = Σphases / cycle
Cycle    = max(60,50,90,80) + 10 = 90 + 10 = 100 ns
One task = 60 + 50 + 90 + 80 = 280 ns
Speedup  = 280 / 100 = 2.8
Pipe 500 = (4 + 500 - 1) x 100 = 503 x 100 = 50 300 ns
Seq 500  = 500 x 280 = 140 000 ns
blocks.answer:
Cycle 100 ns; one task 280 ns; speedup 2.8; 500 tasks pipelined
50 300 ns against sequential 140 000 ns.

blocks.label: Hazards in full: structural, data, and the three orderings
blocks.tag: what forwarding fixes and what it cannot
blocks.html:
A stall is the delay in cycles caused by a hazard, and it feeds straight into the speedup:

speedup with stalls = [1 / (1 + stalls per instruction)] x number of stages

The cycles needed to fill the pipe can be folded into that average stall figure too.

Structural hazards: two instructions, one piece of hardware

When more than one instruction in the pipeline needs to access the same resource, the datapath has a structural hazard. The resources in question are the register file, memory and the ALU.

The classic illustration is one instruction fetching while another reads data, and the underlying problem is stated plainly: there is only one memory port.

The solution: stall the pipeline for one clock cycle when the conflict is detected. That gap has a name: a pipeline bubble.

The same idea appears again as resource constraints: if one common memory serves both data and instructions and you need to read or write while fetching, only one can proceed and the other waits. Or a limited resource such as an execution unit may simply be busy at the moment it is wanted.

Data hazards are different: nothing is contended, but an instruction depends on the result of a previous one. It cannot start until that result comes back, or both try to modify the same data object.

Watch it happen.

ADD R1, R2, R3     ; result goes into R1
SUB R4, R5, R1     ; uses R1
AND R6, R1, R7     ; uses R1
OR  R8, R1, R9     ; uses R1
XOR R10, R1, R11   ; uses R1

Every one of the next four instructions wants the R1 the first has not finished writing.

Forwarding, and why it works

Data hazards are usually solved by data or register forwarding, also called bypassing or short-circuiting.

The trick: the data selected in ID is not really used in ID. It is used in the next stage, the ALU. So the ALU result is fed back from the EX/MEM buffer to the ALU input latches, and if the forwarding hardware sees that a source operand has a newer value in flight, it selects that instead of the register file value.

The answer never went to the register file and back. It went sideways.

How far back does it reach? Results must be forwarded not only from the immediately previous instruction but from any instruction that started up to three cycles before.

  • From EX/MEM, one cycle before, to both ALU inputs.
  • From MEM/WB, two cycles before, to both ALU inputs.
  • Three cycles before is covered by a timing trick: the register file is written in the first half of the cycle and read in the second half, so the value is already there.

Why it is needed, in clock numbers. Take add $s0, $t0, $t1 followed by sub $t2, $s0, $t3, where $s0 is minus 5 before the add and 8 after it. The add writes $s0 in clock 5, but the sub reads $s0 in clock 3. So CC3 reads minus 5, the stale value, when it needed 8. The correct value only exists at the end of clock 5, so the dependency arrow runs from CC5 back to CC3: backward in time, which is exactly why it cannot be satisfied by waiting.

The one forwarding cannot fix

LW R1, 0(R2) followed by SUB R4, R1, R5.

A load's data is not available until MEM/WB. The subtract needs it in EX, which is earlier. There is nothing to forward yet, so the subtract's ALU cycle must be stalled, introducing a vertical bubble.

This is the load-use hazard, and it is the reason schedulers exist.

And the fix for that. Move an independent instruction between the dependent pair. Given

I1  LOAD R1, 0(R2)
I2  ADD  R3, R1, R4     ; depends on I1, stalls
I3  SUB  R5, R6, R7     ; independent
I4  MUL  R8, R3, R9

reorder to LOAD, SUB, ADD, MUL. The SUB fills the delay slot and the stall disappears. Nothing was removed; the order was changed.

The three orderings, which the exam asks you to name and classify.

NameMeaningStatus
RAWRead After WriteThe most common, a true dependency, solved by data forwarding
WAWWrite After Write: instruction i, a load, and instruction j, an add, both write the same registerCannot happen in DLX, because DLX waits for WB to write registers. It appears in complex instruction sets with auto-increment modes that read operands late
WARWrite After Read: j writes a destination before i has read it, so i gets the wrong valueCannot happen in DLX, since all instructions read early in ID and write late in WB

Worked classification, and this exact shape is set as an exercise.

I1  ADD R1, R2, R3
I2  SUB R4, R1, R5
I3  MUL R1, R6, R7
I4  DIV R8, R1, R9
  • I1 to I2: I2 reads R1 after I1 wrote it, so RAW
  • I1 to I3: I3 writes R1 after I1 wrote it, so WAW
  • I3 to I4: I4 reads R1 after I3 wrote it, so RAW

The method never changes: find the register that appears on both lines, then read the order of write and read. Never classify by the instruction names. The exercise asks you to describe all three and mark each occurrence with an arrow, so draw the arrow from the earlier instruction to the later one.

Where the topic lands. By dividing execution into stages and overlapping them, pipelining increases throughput and makes better use of CPU resources. The hazards and synchronisation problems are real, and modern systems answer them with sophisticated hardware and software techniques to reduce delays. As processor technology evolves, pipelining remains a foundational concept in high-performance computing.

blocks.label: Worked example
blocks.problem: A non-pipelined processor takes 60 ns per instruction. Redesigned as a 6-stage pipeline with a 12 ns cycle time, running 50 instructions. Find both times and the speedup. (This is the one question on the revision deck that is not on any past paper, so learn it fresh.)
blocks.working:
Given non-pipelined 60 ns/instruction · k = 6 stages · cycle 12 ns · n = 50
Formula non-pipe = n × time/instruction · pipe = (k + n − 1) × cycle · speedup = non-pipe / pipe
Without pipelining = 50 x 60 = 3000 ns
With pipelining    = (6 + 50 - 1) x 12
                   = 55 x 12
                   = 660 ns      (fill 6x12=72, then 49x12=588)
Speedup            = 3000 / 660 = 4.55
blocks.answer: Without pipelining 3000 ns; with pipelining 660 ns; speedup 4.55.
blocks.redo: Now redo it: n × per-instruction time without, (k + n − 1) × cycle with, then divide.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto: Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Overlapping is not free: sometimes two instructions in the pipe clash, and a clash is called a hazard. There are three kinds, and you must be able to name them. The first is the structural hazard, where two instructions need the same piece of hardware in the same cycle (one memory wanted for a fetch and a data access at once).
frames.ask: How do you remove a structural hazard?

frames.teach: (for example, separate instruction and data memories, so each instruction has its own). The second kind is the data hazard: an instruction needs a result that an earlier instruction has not written yet. We name its three types by the order in which two instructions touch the same register.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: RAW (read after write) is the true dependency: the second instruction reads a register the first has not written yet. It is eased by forwarding, which feeds the result straight from where it is produced to where it is needed, before the write-back stage.
frames.ask: Which of the three data hazards is the real dependency?

frames.teach: The other two, WAR (write after read) and WAW (write after write), are only naming clashes over the same register, not true data flow.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: When forwarding cannot deliver the value in time, the pipeline must stall: it inserts a bubble, an idle cycle, until the value is ready.
frames.ask: What is the idle cycle a stall inserts called?

frames.teach: The third kind is the control hazard: a branch changes which instruction runs next, but the pipe has already fetched the ones right after the branch. It is eased by branch prediction and speculative execution, whose whole purpose is to reduce control-hazard stalls.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now classify one pair. The first instruction writes R3, and the second instruction reads R3. The shared register is R3, and the order is write then read.
frames.ask: Which data hazard is that?

frames.teach: (write then read is exactly read-after-write). That is every hazard idea in place. The box just below shows how to draw the pipeline timing diagram the paper sometimes asks for; after it, sit the two "your turn" boxes with the answers covered.

blocks.label: Teach
blocks.tag: How to draw the timing (cycle) diagram
blocks.html:
The paper sometimes says "draw the pipeline timing diagram" or "draw the cycle diagram". It is always the same grid, and you draw it the same way every time:

  • Cycles across the top (1, 2, 3, ...), one instruction per row down the side.
  • In each cell write the stage that instruction is in that cycle: IF, ID, EX, (MEM), WB. Some papers add an operand fetch (OF) stage between ID and EX; use whatever stages the question names.
  • Each instruction begins its IF one cycle after the instruction above it.
  • A multi-cycle execute (say a 3-cycle multiply or a 6-cycle divide) writes EX in that many cells in a row, and everything behind it slides right.
  • A stall (waiting for a hazard to clear, or for a busy stage) is a gap you mark with a bubble, written --.

The total number of cycles is simply the column where the last instruction reaches WB. That is your answer to "how many cycles".

How to remember it: "cycles across, instructions down, stages in the boxes, count to the last WB." A long EX pushes; a stall is a --. (You will draw exactly this for Question Two and Question Three in the final mock.)

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Find the one register on both lines and read its order. (i) R3 ← R1 op R2, then R5 ← R3 op R4. (ii) R3 ← R1 op R2, then R1 ← R4 op R5. (iii) R3 ← R1 op R2, then R3 ← R6 op R7.
blocks.answer: (i) R3 is written then read, so RAW. (ii) R1 is read then written, so WAR. (iii) R3 is written then written, so WAW. Only RAW is a real data dependency; the other two are naming clashes.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: (1) The main objective of branch prediction and speculative execution is to? (2) A read-after-write clash is eased by which technique?
blocks.answer: (1) reduce pipeline stalls caused by control hazards (keep the pipe full across branches). (2) forwarding (feed the result straight to where it is needed).

blocks.label: Trap
blocks.html: The clock runs at the slowest stage plus latch, not the average or the sum. For n tasks the count is k + n − 1, so 500 tasks in a 4-stage pipe is 503 cycles, not 504. Classify data hazards by the shared register and the order it is written and read, never by the instruction name.

blocks.big: "Clock = the slowest stage + latch. For n tasks it is (k + n − 1) cycles."
blocks.sub: Speedup tops out at k stages. Name a data hazard by the register order: RAW (read after write, the real one, eased by forwarding), WAR, WAW. A long execute pushes everything behind it; a stall is a bubble.

title: Memory and Cache
lead: The memory hierarchy carries the largest single block of objective questions, and cache mapping is the most examined calculation on the whole course. It looks fiddly, so we do it as a programme: many tiny steps, and you check each one before moving on. By the end the cache split will be the same four moves every time.

blocks.label: Work it frame by frame
blocks.tag: cover, work, then slide down to check
blocks.howto:
Cover the page just below the first line with a card or your hand. Read a frame, do
the small task, then slide the card down to the next line to check your answer. One step at a
time, and do not skip.

frames.teach: Memory is arranged in levels, fastest to slowest: registers, then cache, then main memory, then secondary storage (disk or SSD).
frames.ask: Of those four, which is the fastest?

frames.teach:
Picture it as your workspace: the few things in
your hands (registers), the book open on your desk (cache), the shelf beside you (main memory), and
the library across campus (disk). You keep what you use most closest, because reaching further
costs time.
frames.ask:
As you climb toward registers, does memory get cheaper or dearer per
bit?

frames.teach:
Climbing up, memory gets faster, smaller, and more
expensive per bit. The reason there are levels at all is a trade-off: you cannot have fast, big and
cheap at once.
frames.ask: So which level has the highest cost per bit?

frames.teach: Now the two kinds of RAM. SRAM (static RAM) is built from flip-flops: fast, needs no refresh, but costly and low density.
frames.ask: Given it is fast but costly, which level is SRAM used for?

frames.teach: DRAM (dynamic RAM) is built from capacitors: dense and cheap, but slower and it needs periodic refresh, so it is used for main memory. (ROM and Flash are non-volatile; RAM, cache and DRAM are volatile, lost on power off.)
frames.ask: Which kind of RAM has to be refreshed?

frames.teach: Two facts the MCQs love: the MAR (memory address register) holds the address being accessed; and access time is how long one access takes, while cycle time is the minimum gap between the starts of two accesses.
frames.ask: A device with 60 ns access and 90 ns cycle can start a new access how often?

frames.teach: (the cycle time, not the access time). Now, why does a small nearby cache help at all? Because programs are predictable, a habit called locality of reference. It comes in two kinds.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Temporal locality: a location used now is likely used again soon (think of a loop counter, read over and over).
frames.ask:
Reusing the same location again
soon is which locality?

frames.teach: Spatial locality: once a location is used, nearby ones are likely used next (stepping through an array). That is exactly why the cache copies a whole block at a time, not one lonely byte.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Two limits to know by name. The memory wall is the widening gap between fast CPUs and slow memory, which is why a processor can still wait on data despite a big cache. Virtual memory lets a program use an address space larger than the physical RAM, with a memory management unit (MMU) translating the addresses.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Now the cache sum itself, gently. Picture the cache as a wall of numbered hooks (the lines), each big enough to hold one block, a short run of consecutive bytes copied from memory together. Far more blocks exist in memory than there are hooks, so many blocks compete for the same hook.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: When the CPU names an address, that address answers three questions, and that is exactly why it splits into three fields. The first, from the low bits, is the offset.
frames.ask:
Which one thing does the offset pick out: which byte in the block,
which hook, or which block?

frames.teach: The middle bits are the index (or set): which hook the block hangs on. The high bits are the tag: which of the many blocks sharing that hook is actually here, stored beside the block and compared on every access.
frames.ask: A tag that matches means what?

frames.teach: (no match is a miss). Now the sizes, in order. Address bits = log2(main memory size). Offset = log2(block size).
frames.ask: A 16-byte block needs how many offset bits?

frames.teach: (log216 = 4). Number of lines = cache size / block size. Index bits (direct mapped) = log2(lines).
frames.ask: A direct-mapped cache with 64 lines needs how many index bits?

frames.teach: (log264 = 6). For a k-way set associative cache, sets = lines / k and set bits = log2(sets); fully associative has no index at all (any block on any hook). Whatever is left over is the tag: tag bits = address bits − index (or set) − offset. The tag directory = lines × tag bits.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach: Last, the average memory access time (AMAT), with hit ratio h, cache time Tc and memory time Tm. Hierarchical (cache first): AMAT = Tc + (1 − h) × Tm. Simultaneous (both at once): AMAT = h × Tc + (1 − h) × Tm.
frames.ask: Read on.

frames.teach:
That is the whole method: address bits from the
memory, offset from the block, lines from cache over block, tag is whatever is left, then the tag
directory and AMAT. Now watch it on real numbers in the three worked examples below, then drill the
six extra caches with a card over each row.

blocks.label: The organs of the CPU, and the wires between them
blocks.html:
Computer organization deals with how architectural features are physically implemented. It has six components, and the exam asks for each by name, with an example of where it matters.

ComponentWhat it doesWhere it shows up in life
Control unitCoordinates all operations of the CPU: fetching instructions, decoding instructions, and generating control signalsEvery program that runs at all; industrial automation, where machines act on control signals; robotics, where it drives sensors and actuators
ALUArithmetic such as addition and subtraction, and logic such as AND, OR and NOTDigital calculators; gaming, whose physics depends on it; artificial intelligence, whose neural networks are massive arithmetic
RegistersSmall, fast storage inside the CPU: general-purpose registers, and special-purpose ones such as the Program Counter and the Stack PointerPrograms run faster with data in registers than in memory; air traffic control depends on it; efficient register use improves battery life on mobiles
Memory organizationArranged hierarchically: cache (fastest), then main memory or RAM, then secondary storageSmartphones, whose app speed depends on it; web browsers, where cache speeds page loading; cloud systems
Input/output systemsHandle communication between the computer and external devicesKeyboard in and monitor out; medical devices, sensors in and displays out; smart homes
BusesTransfer data, addresses and control signalsMotherboards, where everything talks over buses; gaming computers, where fast buses lift graphics; servers
The three buses, and the division of labour

Data bus carries the value.
Address bus carries which location is wanted.
Control bus carries the signals that say read or write, and when.

Three questions about any transfer: what, where, and when. One bus each.

And the seventh item on the organization list, which gets its own lesson later: pipelining is the overlapping of instruction execution, while parallelism is the executing of multiple tasks simultaneously. Modern CPUs run several instructions at once, multicore processors give real multitasking, and AI and big-data systems lean on both.

Read that list against the architecture list from Part A and the split is exact: architecture named the instruction set, data types, addressing modes and registers a program can see. Organization names the control unit, the ALU, the memory organization, the I/O systems, the buses and the pipelining. Nothing appears twice.

blocks.label: How memory is reached, and what it costs
blocks.html:
Memory has a set of characteristics the lecture lists: its location, its access method, its performance such as transfer rate, and its capacity or size. Start with the access methods, because each has a device attached to it.

MethodHow it reaches a locationExample
SequentialReads locations one after another, in sequenceMagnetic tape
RandomAll locations accessible in constant timeRAM
DirectLike locating a street: find the vicinity or block first, then search within itHard disk drive
AssociativeHolds the address and the content together, so you search by contentCache

Remember them by the device, not the definition. Tape has to wind, so sequential. RAM is the R in its own name. A disk head swings to a track then waits, so direct. And cache has to answer "do you have address X?" without being told where to look, so associative.

The three design constraints, as three questions

How much space? If memory exists, applications will likely be developed to use it.
How fast is the access time? Best performance is when memory keeps up with the processor, so the processor is not left pausing or waiting for instructions or operands.
How expensive? The cost must be reasonable in relation to other components.

The trade-off that makes all three impossible at once:

  • Faster access time means greater cost per bit.
  • Greater capacity means slower access.
  • Smaller cost per bit means slower access.

So the way out is not a single memory. It is a memory hierarchy: a structured arrangement of different storage types designed to optimize performance and cost, supplementing smaller, more expensive, faster memories with larger, cheaper, slower ones.

Going down the hierarchy, three things fall and two rise: cost per bit decreases, capacity increases, access time increases, and, the one that makes the whole scheme work, the frequency of access by the processor decreases.

The in-class question

Why do we not use only cache memory in a computer system?

Because cache is very expensive and has limited capacity. A machine built entirely of cache would be superb and unaffordable, and too small to hold anything.

blocks.label: Locality of reference, and why 95 per cent is nearly all of it
blocks.problem: Level 1 holds 1000 words with an access time of 0.01 microseconds. Level 2 holds 100,000 words at 0.1 microseconds. If 95 per cent of accesses are found in L1, what is the average access time?
blocks.working:
First, why any of this works at all. The hierarchy would be useless if programs jumped about memory at random. They do not, and the reason has a name.

LocalityWhat it saysWhere it comes from
SpatialIf we access a location, close by addresses will very likely be accessedMarching along an array in a loop
TemporalIf we access a location, we will very likely access it againThe loop counter, read every pass

Both are a consequence of using iterative loops and subroutines, because instructions and data get accessed many times over.

Step 1: what each access costs

  • Word is in L1: the processor accesses it directly, 0.01 microseconds
  • Word is in L2: it is first transferred to L1, then accessed, so 0.01 + 0.1

Note the miss cost includes the L1 time as well. You still read it from L1 in the end. The time to work out which level holds the word is ignored, for simplicity.

Step 2: name the symbols

SymbolMeaning
HThe fraction of all accesses found in L1
T1Access time to L1
T2Access time to L2

Step 3: weigh the two cases

average = 0.95 x 0.01  +  0.05 x (0.01 + 0.1)= 0.0095 + 0.0055= 0.015 microseconds
Look at where that answer sits

L1 costs 0.01 and L2 costs 0.11, yet the average is 0.015, almost on top of L1.

For high percentages of L1 access, the average is much closer to L1 than to L2. That is the whole justification for the hierarchy: you do not need to be right every time, only nearly every time.

And the strategy that produces the 95 per cent: organize the data across the levels so the percentage of accesses to lower levels is substantially less than to upper ones. L2 holds all program instructions and data; data currently in use is held in L1; and eventually L1 data is swapped out to L2 to make room. On average, most references land in L1.
blocks.answer: 0.015 microseconds, far closer to L1 than to L2
blocks.redo: Redo it at a 50 per cent hit rate: 0.5 x 0.01 + 0.5 x 0.11 = 0.005 + 0.055 = 0.06 microseconds, four times worse. Then try 99 per cent: 0.0099 + 0.0011 = 0.011, nearly L1 exactly. Plot those three in your head and you can see why cache designers fight so hard for the last few per cent of hit rate.

blocks.label: Cache in detail: hit, miss, lines, tags and the bus
blocks.tag: the heaviest topic on the paper
blocks.html:
Three levels, said precisely. Processor registers are the fastest, smallest and most expensive memory. Main memory is the principal internal memory system, and each of its locations has a unique address. Between them sits the cache, which stages data movement between registers and main memory, improves performance, and is not usually visible to the processor or the programmer.

What cache is for, in one sentence

Cache is designed to combine the access time of expensive, high-speed memory with the size of less expensive, lower-speed memory. It does that by holding a copy of portions of main memory.

Typical sizes make the point: cache 1 to 2 MB, main memory up to 64 GB.

The units, since questions are set in them. A nibble is 4 bits, a byte is 8 bits, a word is one or more complete rows of memory, and a block is a collection of words, typically 2, 4 or 8.

SizeWorkingBits
4 MB4 x 1024 x 1024 x 833,554,432
10 KB10 x 1024 x 881,920

Now the operation, and it is four lines.

  1. The processor generates the read address RA of the word it wants.
  2. A check is made to see whether the word is in the cache.
  3. Hit: the word is delivered to the processor.
  4. Miss: the block of main memory containing the word is read into the cache, and the cache then delivers the word. Those last two happen in parallel.

Why fetch a whole block for one word? Because of locality of reference: once a block is in the cache it is likely there will be future references to that same location, and to its neighbours.

How the two sides are counted

Main memory has 2n addressable words, each with a unique n-bit address, organised into fixed-length blocks of K words each. So the number of blocks is
M = 2n / K

Cache has m blocks, called LINES. Each line holds K words and some control bits.

Because m is much less than M, the cache cannot permanently hold any block, so it must identify which block it is currently holding. That identification is the tag field.

And when a word in a block is read, the whole block is transferred to a cache line. Line, not block, is the word to use on the cache side.

What happens on the bus, which is examined directly. The cache connects to the processor by data, control and address lines. The data and address lines also attach to data and address buffers, which attach to a system bus leading to main memory.

EventWhat happens on the bus
Cache hitThe data and address buffers are disabled. Communication is only between processor and cache. There is no system bus traffic
Cache missThe desired address is loaded onto the system bus, and the data return through the data buffer to both the cache and the processor

That is the real benefit stated in hardware terms: a hit does not merely save time, it keeps the system bus free for everything else.

Multiple levels. The idea improves by adding more: L2 is slower and typically larger than L1, and L3 is slower and typically larger than L2. The same trade repeated at each step.

Physical against logical addresses

Physical addresses are actual memory addresses. Logical addresses are virtual-memory addresses.

Virtual memory performs the mapping between the logical addresses a program uses and physical addresses, and its main idea is to disregard the amount of main memory available, so a program can be written as though memory were unlimited.

A virtual cache stores data using logical addresses, so the processor reaches it without going through the MMU.

AdvantageDisadvantage
Faster access, since the cache can respond without an MMU address translationThe same virtual address in two applications refers to two different physical addresses. So the cache must be flushed at every context switch, or extra bits added to each line to say which virtual address space the address belongs to

Finally, how big should a cache be? Two bounds, pulling opposite ways:

  • Small enough that the overall average cost per bit is close to main memory alone.
  • Large enough that the overall average access time is close to the cache alone.

And a third pressure: the larger the cache, the more complex the addressing logic, so large caches tend to be slightly slower than small ones. Available chip and board area limits it further.

blocks.label: The three mapping functions, and why a mapping is needed at all
blocks.html:
Start with the arithmetic of the problem. There are far fewer cache lines than main memory blocks. Sixty-four lines, say, and thousands of blocks. So a rule is needed to decide which line a given block is allowed to occupy. That rule is the mapping function, and there are three techniques: direct, associative and set associative.

One piece of vocabulary before the detail: block size, frame size and line size all mean the same thing in these questions. The examiner uses them interchangeably and expects you to follow.

1. Direct mapping: one block, one possible line

The simplest technique. Each block of main memory maps into only one possible cache line, given by

i = j modulo m
where i is the cache line number, j is the main memory block number, and m is the number of lines in the cache.

Modulo is the clue: block 0, block m, block 2m and so on all land on line 0. Like house numbers on a street of m hooks, going round and round.

How a lookup works. Use the line field of the memory address to index the cache line, then compare the tag from the address with the tag stored in that line.

  • Tags match: a hit, and the word is retrieved from that indexed line.
  • Tags do not match: a miss, and the indexed line is updated with the word and the tag.
AdvantageDisadvantage
Simple and inexpensive to implement. One index, one comparisonThere is a fixed location for any given block. If a program repeatedly references words from two different blocks that map to the same line, those blocks are continually swapped and the hit ratio collapses. That is thrashing
2. Associative mapping: any block, any line

It overcomes the disadvantage of direct mapping by permitting each main memory block to be loaded into any line of the cache.

With no fixed line, there is no index field. The control logic reads an address as just two parts: a Tag of s bits, which uniquely identifies a block of main memory, and a Word field of w bits, which identifies a word inside the block.

The cost of that freedom. To find out whether a block is present, the control logic must simultaneously examine EVERY line's tag for a match. That is a lot of comparators, which is why fully associative caches are small and expensive.

  • Match: a hit, and the tag field is used to index the line and retrieve the word.
  • No match: a miss, and a line must be chosen, then updated with the word and the tag.

Notice the extra decision on a miss. Direct mapping never has to choose, because there is only one candidate. Associative mapping must pick a victim, which is why replacement policies exist at all.

3. Set associative: the compromise that is actually used

An enhanced form of direct mapping in which its drawbacks are removed, and specifically the thrashing problem.

Instead of exactly one line per block, a few lines are grouped into a SET, and a memory block can map to any one line of its specific set.

So each index address can now hold two or more words from main memory at once. It combines the best of the direct and associative techniques: a short search, but no forced eviction when two hot blocks collide.

MappingAddress splits intoHow many tags to compare
DirectTag, Index, OffsetOne
Fully associativeTag, Offset. No indexAll of them
n-way set associativeTag, Set index, Offsetn, the ones in that set

Read the middle column down and the whole topic is there. Every bit you take off the index has to go somewhere, and it goes into the tag. That is why a fully associative cache has the longest tags and the biggest tag directory.

blocks.label: The same cache, mapped three ways
blocks.tag: 16 KB cache, 256 B block, 128 KB memory
blocks.problem: A cache of 16 KB with block size 256 bytes serves a main memory of 128 KB. Find the tag bits and the tag directory size when the cache is direct mapped, fully associative, and 2-way set associative.
blocks.working:
Step 0: the two numbers that never change, whatever the mapping

Memory is taken to be byte addressable throughout.

QuantityWorkingResult
Physical address128 KB = 217 bytes17 bits
Block offset256 B = 28 bytes8 bits
Lines in cache16 KB / 256 B = 214 / 28 = 2664 lines

Those three come from the sizes alone. The mapping decides only what happens to the bits that are left over.

Case 1: DIRECT mapped

64 lines is 26, so the line number takes 6 bits.

tag = 17 - (6 + 8) = 17 - 14 = 3 bitstag directory = lines x tag = 26 x 3 = 192 bits = 24 bytes

Case 2: FULLY ASSOCIATIVE

There is no index at all, so nothing is subtracted but the offset.

tag = 17 - 8 = 9 bitstag directory = 26 x 9 = 576 bits = 72 bytes

Three times the tag directory of the direct case, for exactly the same cache. The six index bits did not vanish; they moved into the tag.

Case 3: 2-WAY SET ASSOCIATIVE

The set size is 2, so the 64 lines group into sets:

sets = lines / set size = 64 / 2 = 32 = 25, so the set number is 5 bitstag = 17 - (5 + 8) = 4 bits

Exactly between the two: one bit more tag than direct, five fewer than fully associative.

The method, once, for any numbers

1. address bits = log2(memory size)
2. offset = log2(block size)
3. lines = cache size / block size
4. index = log2(lines)  |  sets = lines / n, set bits = log2(sets)  |  fully associative: none
5. tag = whatever is left
6. tag directory = lines x tag bits

And reading one real address. In that last cache the CPU issues 000010 000011 1001. Split it by the field widths, 6 then 6 then 4:

  • tag = 000010 = 2
  • index = 000011 = 3
  • offset = 1001 = 9

So: go to line 3, check whether its stored tag is 2, and if it is, take byte 9 of that line.

The same 64 KB / 1 KB / 16 B cache, made fully associative: the offset stays 4 bits, the tag becomes 16 - 4 = 12 bits, there are still 1024/16 = 64 lines, and the tag directory is 64 x 12 = 768 bits, that is 96 bytes. Made 2-way set associative instead: 64 lines give 32 sets, so the set index is 5 bits, the tag is 16 - 5 - 4 = 7 bits, and the directory is 7 x 64 = 448 bits, that is 56 bytes.

The fully associative tag stays at 9, because it never depended on the line count, and only its directory grows. That contrast is the fastest way to check you have understood which quantity depends on what.

title: RISC, CISC and the Rest
lead: Two design philosophies, plus the loose theory ideas the objective test dips into. Mostly describing and comparing, so we do it as a short programme: one small contrast at a time, then check. Get the contrasts clean and these are fast, reliable marks.

blocks.label: Why two philosophies exist at all
blocks.html:
First, the vocabulary. A processor is the logic circuitry that responds to and processes the basic instructions that drive a computer. Those CPU instructions are numbers stored in memory, nothing more exotic. An instruction set is the set of instructions a programmer can give a machine to perform operations, and it is specific to the CPU architecture.

Whatever the design, the basic operations of a processor are always these four:

  1. Read the instruction from memory
  2. Decode it
  3. Execute it
  4. Write back the result
The whole argument in one sentence

Given those four steps, should one instruction do a lot, or should each do very little but very fast?

The two answers are CISC, the Complex Instruction Set Computer, and RISC, the Reduced Instruction Set Computer. Neither is wrong. They were right at different times, for reasons of cost.

The 1960s and 1970s: memory was expensive, processor hardware was relatively cheap.

Read that sentence again, because everything follows from it. If memory costs more than logic, the sensible move is to make programs smaller, even if the chip has to work harder. So engineers built processors with powerful instructions capable of performing complex tasks in a single instruction. That is how CISC arrived.

The in-class question, and its answer. Why were CISC architectures initially popular? Because memory was expensive, and CISC instructions could perform complex operations using fewer instructions, thereby reducing program size.

Two more reasons from the same era:

  • The earliest machines were programmed in assembly language by hand, with slow and expensive memory. IBM designed an instruction set to let early programmers write a hundred complex instructions rather than thousands of individual ones.
  • CISC was developed to make compiler development simpler: it shifts most of the burden of generating machine instructions to the processor. Rather than a compiler emitting a long sequence to calculate a square root, a CISC processor would have that built in.
Then the early 1980s, and two measurements changed everything

1. Researchers discovered that most programs used only a small subset of the available instructions. All that complexity was sitting unused.
2. They found complex instructions often required multiple clock cycles, while simpler instructions could be executed much faster.

Those two observations led to RISC.

Both live on, and the split is visible in your pocket: computers typically use CISC, while tablets, smartphones and other devices use RISC. The higher efficiency of RISC makes it desirable where cycles and power are in short supply, which is exactly a device running on a battery.

blocks.label: CISC in full: what it is, what it buys, what it costs
blocks.html:
Complex instruction set computing is a CPU design where single instructions can execute several low-level operations, such as a load from memory, an arithmetic operation and a memory store all at once, or which are capable of multi-step operations or addressing modes within a single instruction.

It is called complex because of the complex work performed per instruction. The concept is to encode the intention directly: add X and Y and put the result in Z, said once.

The numbers the exam asks for
CharacteristicTypical figure
Number of instructions100 to 250
Addressing modes5 to 20
General purpose registersA small number
Cycles per instructionGenerally more than 1

Its characteristics and properties, as listed. Variable-length instruction formats; instructions that manipulate operands in memory; some instructions performing specialized tasks used infrequently; a richer instruction set, some simple and some very complex; instructions of variable size; interfacing with memory in multiple mechanisms with complex addressing modes; and no pipelining.

How the instructions are actually carried out: in CISC, instructions are executed by microcode. Microcode control is what makes the CISC instruction set possible and flexible, and it is why CISC works well with a simpler compiler.

Advantages of CISCDisadvantages of CISC
Microprogramming is as easy as assembly language to implement, and much less expensive than hardwiring a control unitThe complex instructions are infrequently used by programmers and compilers
As each instruction became more capable, fewer instructions were needed for a task, making more efficient use of slow main memoryMemory references, loads and stores are slow, and account for a significant fraction of all instructions
Micro-program instruction sets can be written to match high-level language constructs, so the compiler need not be as complicatedProcedure and function calls are a major bottleneck: passing arguments, storing and retrieving values in registers
Some instructions take more time than others, and the instruction set and chip grow more complex with each generation

Examples of CISC architectures: x86 and s390.

CISC multiplying 5 by 10, in three instructions
Mov ax, 10
Mov bx, 5
Mul bx

Load, load, and one instruction that does the whole multiplication. Short to write, and the hardware carries the weight. Compare it with the RISC version in the next section and the entire trade-off is visible in two code listings.

blocks.label: RISC in full: fewer instructions, one cycle each
blocks.html:
Where it came from. The first RISC projects came from IBM, Stanford and UC-Berkeley in the late 70s and early 80s: the IBM 801, Stanford MIPS, and Berkeley RISC 1 and 2.

The insight behind all three

Three main factors affect processor performance:
1. how fast you can crank up the clock
2. how much work you can do per cycle
3. how many instructions you need to perform a task

CISC attacked the third. RISC decided the first two were worth far more, and that the third could be paid for.

Watch the trade in one example. Instead of the single complex instruction MULT A, B, RISC writes:

LOAD R1, A
LOAD R2, B
MUL R3, R1, R2
STORE R3, C

Four instructions instead of one. But each executes very quickly, and that is the bargain.

It is called reduced not because there are fewer instructions in the program, but because of the reduction of work performed by an instruction. RISC is a microprocessor architecture that uses a small, highly-optimized set of instructions rather than a specialized set. Its original goal was to limit the number of instructions on the chip so that each could be allocated enough transistors to execute in one cycle.

Load-store, and why it matters

The small instruction set consists mostly of register-to-register operations, with only simple load and store operations for memory access.

So: each operand is brought into a register by a load, all computation happens among registers, and results are returned to memory by a store. Memory is touched twice, at the beginning and the end, and never in the middle.

Why: registers can transfer information to other registers much faster than information can move to and from memory.

The rest of the design follows from that decision.

  • Few addressing modes, because almost all instructions use simple register addressing, though modes such as immediate operands may be included.
  • A simple instruction format, so the instruction length can be fixed and aligned on word boundaries, and above all easy to decode.
  • Shorter instructions, breaking a complex instruction into several short simple ones.
  • The ability to execute one instruction per clock cycle, achieved by overlapping the fetch, decode and execute phases of two or three instructions, which is pipelining.
  • Hardwired control rather than microcode, with complexity pushed to the compiler.
Advantages of RISCDisadvantages of RISC
Often 2 to 4 times the performance of CISC using comparable semiconductor technology and the same clock ratesCode quality: performance depends greatly on the code. If the programmer or compiler schedules instructions poorly, the processor stalls, waiting for one result before it can proceed
Much less chip space and simple hardware requirements, since the instruction set is so simpleCode expansion: where a CISC machine performs a complex action in one instruction, RISC may need several
Shorter design cycle: simpler chips are designed more quickly, and complete their work in 1 clock cycleIt requires very fast memory to feed its instructions, so RISC systems typically carry large caches on the chip itself, known as a first-level cache
RISC multiplying 5 by 10, with no multiply instruction at all

Because the designers make sure add executes in one clock, a compiler can multiply a by b by adding a to itself b times:

Mov ax, 0
Mov bx, 10
Mov cx, 5
Begin:
  Add ax, bx
  Loop Begin

Far more instructions than the CISC version. Each one costs a single cycle, and the loop pipelines cleanly, which is how it wins the race anyway.

blocks.label: The comparison table, and the second in-class question
blocks.html:
The in-class question: Why is pipelining more difficult in CISC processors?

The answer, in the words the marker wants

Because CISC instructions have varying lengths and execution times, which makes it harder to process instructions uniformly through the pipeline stages.

A pipeline is an assembly line. An assembly line only works if every item takes the same time at every station.

The summary comparisons, as the deck states them.

PointCISCRISC
Cycles usedInstructions utilize more cyclesUsually one cycle
Instruction complexityMore complexSimpler

Designed forGood performance on slow memoriesA good cost to performance ratio

Read the last two rows together and the whole history is there. CISC was optimised for the constraint of its era, expensive slow memory. RISC was optimised for the constraint of ours, cycles and power. Neither designer was wrong.

And where each ends up: computers typically use CISC; tablets, smartphones and similar devices use RISC, because its higher efficiency is what you want when cycles and power are in short supply.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: a. i) Computer Systems are designed using two closely related but distinct concepts which are Computer Architecture and Computer Organization. Differentiate between these concepts. 2mks ii) Compare Von Neumann Architecture and Harvard Architecture. Include a diagram for each. 3mks

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
i) Differentiate computer architecture from computer organization.

Computer architecture is defined as the functional design and logical structure of the computer system as the programmer sees it: the instruction set, the data types, the addressing modes and the register organization. It answers the question "What does the computer do?" and serves as the blueprint for the system.

Computer organization is defined as the operational units and their interconnections that realize (carry out) that architecture: the control signals, the buses, the memory technology used and the cache. It answers the question "How does the computer do it?" A useful likeness: architecture is the building's design, organization is the actual construction of the building.

ii) Compare Von Neumann and Harvard architecture, with a diagram for each.

Von Neumann architecture is defined as a design that uses a single (shared) area of memory, reached over one bus, for both the program instructions and the data those instructions act on. It is simple to build, but the shared path is a bottleneck (an instruction fetch and a data access cannot happen at the same instant).

Harvard architecture is defined as a design that uses separate memories and separate buses for instructions and data, which lets it fetch an instruction and read data at the same time (a form of parallelism), at the cost of duplicating the address, data and control lines.

blocks.label: As printed
blocks.printed: b. A computer manufacturer is evaluating whether to replace a non-pipelined processor with a five-stage pipelined processor. Pipelined processor stage times are: IF – 5ns, ID – 4ns, EX – 6ns, MEM – 5ns and WB – 4ns. Furthermore, Pipeline register overhead is 1 ns. Branch instructions incur a two-cycle penalty, Floating-point instructions has three cycles for EX stage, Memory accesses experience cache misses 10% of the time, adding four extra cycles. The program contains 20 million instructions. i) Determine the pipelined clock cycle. 1mk ii) Calculate the actual CPI. 2mks iii) Determine the actual execution time. 1mk iv) Compute the speedup over the non-pipelined processor. 1mk v) Explain why the speedup differs from the theoretical maximum. 1mk

Formula clock = slowest stage + overhead · actual CPI = 1 + Σ(fraction × extra cycles) · time = IC × CPI × T · speedup = time(non-pipe) / time(pipe)

The stem is dense and does not say whether each penalty is extra or total, so state the reading: base CPI 1; branch +2; memory +(2 + 0.10×4) = 2.4; floating point +4; arithmetic +0.

       = 6 + 1 = 7 ns

blocks.label: In the hall
blocks.working:
i) Locality of reference is defined as the tendency of a program to keep accessing the same small set of memory locations over a short period, a consequence of loops and subroutines; it is why a small fast cache can satisfy most accesses.

ii) Temporal (time) locality is defined as: if a memory location is accessed, it is very likely to be accessed again soon (the same instruction or variable reused). Its partner, spatial (space) locality, is defined as: if a location is accessed, the nearby addresses are very likely to be accessed next (as when stepping through an array).

blocks.answer: (i) Locality of reference is the tendency of a program to access a small, predictable set of memory locations during any short period. Temporal: a location used now is likely to be used again soon, so cache keeps recently used items. Spatial: locations near one just used are likely to be used soon, so cache fetches a whole block of neighbours at once. (ii) On a miss the word is not in cache, so the address goes onto the system bus, main memory returns the whole block containing it, that block is loaded into a cache line (evicting one if necessary), and the required word is delivered to the CPU at the same time.

Trap describing the bottleneck as "the CPU is faster than memory". That is a different problem. The bottleneck named here is the single shared path that instructions and data must both travel, so no instruction fetch and data access can happen in the same instant.
blocks.answer: The Von Neumann concept: a computer stores its program (instructions) and its data together in the same memory, and executes instructions one after another by fetching them from that memory. Two aspects: (a) a single shared memory holds both instructions and data; (b) instructions execute sequentially, one at a time, under the stored-program idea. The bottleneck: because one bus is shared between instructions and data, the CPU cannot fetch an instruction and access data at the same instant, so that single path limits overall speed however fast the CPU is.

title: The Night Before, on One Page
lead:
The whole course compressed to one hook and the key formula for each skill. If you
can rebuild a row from memory, you own it; if you cannot, flip back to that section. Read this
last tonight, and once more walking in.

blocks.html:
SkillRemember this
Number systemsPowers of the base, right to left; 4 bits = 1 hex digit. To decimal: digit × place, then add. To another base: divide, read remainders bottom to top.
Signed numbersFlip and add one, to write a negative and to read one. Add the patterns, drop the top carry. Range −2n−1 to 2n−1 − 1.
IEEE-754Sign, exponent, mantissa (1 + 8 + 23, bias 127). value = ± 1.M × 2(field − 127). Hide the leading 1.
Image sizingpixels = inches × dpi; bits = pixels × depth; bytes = bits ÷ 8; MB = ÷ 1024 twice.
Architecture vs organizationArchitecture = the blueprint (what, the ISA); organization = the construction (how). Von Neumann shares one memory, Harvard splits the two.

SkillRemember this
InstructionsOpcode = what, operands = what to. Fewer addresses, shorter but more of them. bytes = opcode + (addresses × bytes each).
Addressing modesCount the hops: immediate 0, direct 1, indirect 2. EA is the place; operand is M[EA]. Indexed, base, relative add to the field.
CPU performanceTime = IC × CPI × T. CPI = Σ(fraction × cycles). Improvement = (old − new)/old. Amdahl S = 1/((1−f) + f/s), ceiling 1/(1−f).
PipeliningClock = slowest stage + latch. n tasks = (k + n − 1) cycles, speedup up to k. Hazards RAW/WAR/WAW by the register order.
Memory and cacheOffset, index, tag = byte, hook, block. offset = log2(block), lines = cache ÷ block, index = log2(lines), tag = the rest. AMAT = Tc + (1−h)×Tm.

SkillRemember this
RISC vs CISCRISC: few, fixed, one-cycle, pipelines cleanly. CISC: many, complex, variable-length. A stable ISA gives backward compatibility; SIMD accelerates data-parallel work.
Sitting the paperQuestion One is compulsory (30 marks), then any two of Questions Two to Five (20 each). Every answer: the Given, the Formula, the working stacked vertically, then the answer. Never write a bare number without its formula above it. Go and pass.
